Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I wish to call attention to the order of business of the House. For the last two or three years, when the government have taken all the days in the week

but one, if the day not taken was other than Wednesday, the order of business for Wednesday was adopted for the day so left free for business introduced by private members. I understand that we have but one day devoted to business introduced by private members under the resolution introduced by the right hon. leader of the government, and that day is Monday ; and I see by the Order paper that the regular Order for this day is retained-that is, we have first, questions to be put by members, next notices of motion, and next public Bills and Orders. Now, notices of motion may occupy the day and so public Bills and Orders be entirely excluded from consideration. Under the regular order of business we have Monday devoted, as under the Order now before us, to questions to be put by members, then notices of motion, then public Bills and Orders; Wednesday to notices of motion up to six o'clock and public Bills and Orders after half-past seven ; and Thursday to public Bills and Orders up to six o'clock, and notices of motion after half-past seven. This divided the time as equally and fairly as it is possible to do between these classes of business-notices of motions and public Bills and Orders. I presume that it is an oversight that the custom of the last two or three years has not been followed and the order of business for Wednesday fixed for Monday. Now, we have on the Order paper nineteen public Bills. If the Order is retained as it stands, we are in danger of not reaching any of these. Some of them are Bills of importance, among them the Bill with regard to the cigarette question.
The government will take that up.

The government may. But then the government may not. This House has affirmed by an overwhelming majority that a certain line of action is desirable with regard to that matter and here is a Bill introduced by the gentleman who introduced that resolution-
Do I understand that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) intends to conclude with a motion.

I will conclude with a motion, if necessary, Mr. Speaker, though I was merely calling attention to the Order of procedure. Here are nineteen public Bills which, under the Order laid down, if it is not amended, will not be reached or taken into consideration during this session. I was pointing out the importance of one of these Bills, that respecting the cigarette question. I think the country will be very much dissatisfied with the course of this House, if, through inadvertence, no action is taken upon that matter. For this reason, I suggest to the government the course that has been adopted for the last two years certainly, and, I think, for the last three years- that the order of business for Wednesday
shall be made the order of business for Monday, making the Order first, question put by members, then notices of motions up to six o'clock, and public Bills and Orders after half-past seven. I move that this House do now adjourn.

This Bill seems likely to go through with the facility which usually attends the passage of Bills of this character through this House. I have had my attention called to this Bill for the first time by seeing it on the Order Paper. It is a Bill entitled ' An Act for the relief of William Francis Schooley.' The Bill sets forth the allegation that this man's wife left him some years ago, went to the United States, obtained a divorce there, is married and is living with the person whom she married in the state of Michigan; and he applies for a divorce and the privilege of marrying again. Now, these circumstances undoubtedly warrant the issue of a decree of divorce. But the question which faces me in this matter is : What do I know about these circumstances 1 I am galled upon to act, as a member of the House of Commons, which either gives or withholds this decree. The decree can be given properly only upon the substantiation of these grounds. If the grounds alleged do not exist, the decree should be withheld. I know nothing about the trial, nothing about the evidence. I am not aware whether there was a cross-examination, whether the evidence was properly brought out, whether there is collusion, whether the allegation is well founded. Under these circumstances the Bill is presented to this House for its ratification. I wish to call attention, as I have done repeatedly before, to the fact that, in my opinion, this whole proceeding is wrong. If cause exists for divorce, that cause should be ascertained by judicial process, and for this purpose the case should be referred to a properly constituted court. There should be no doubt resting upon the mind of any individual who is called upon to register a decree with reference to such a matter. But, in this case, I feel that sense of doubt. I do not wish to do injustice to one party; on the other hand, I do not wish to do injustice to the other party. Yet, in a broad sense, I know nothing about the case except the representation that is made here, that a commitee of the Senate has had the matter under consideration and has seen fit to report favourably upon this Bill. I protest against this line of action. I protest against being called upon as a member of this House of Commons to record my verdict in this matter. The whole system of grant-73
ing divorces in cases outside the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is based upon a fallacious arrangement. I repeat that this is a judicial case that should pertain to a judicial tribunal; that the Act should issue only upon evidence which, under the law would warrant a divorce. As soon as possible we should get rid of this expensive, this antiquated, this absurd system of granting divorces. We should establish a divorce court, set forth clearly in the law the conditions under which a divorce may be granted ; then, let it be ascertained by 'the tribunal whether the circumstances as established by the evidence, are such as to warrant the granting of a divorce under the law.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

1.	George Swinehammer, keeper of the light at Peggy's Gove, Halifax county, was relieved from his position as light-keeper on account of his advanced age, and loss of activity consequent thereon. At the time Mr. Swinehammer was released, he was 74 years of age, and the department was informed officially that on account of the want of physical activity and intelligence consequent upon his age lie was not adapted to act as keeper of a light of that order. It appears that lighting apparatus of a very improved character was adopted at this station, and that for the want of the qualifications mentioned an explosion occurred, and the apparatus was partially destroyed. The department was forced to the conclusion that in the interest of the public service it was necessary to appoint a younger and more active man.

speechtext:
I am quite aware that there is a large difference in regard to the size. At the same time, it seems to me that this difference does not justify in any way the enormous discrepancies! in the estimated quantities of earth and rock excavation. I happen to know that only at the town of Port Hope is there any rock excavation whatever, and Mr. Rogers, in his report, simply expresses a doubt as to whether there would be any large amount of rock excavation to be done in getting rid of the height of land a short distance from Rice lake. It is mere guess work, so far as I can see. I do not think he could have made a careful survey, or his quantities would have been expressed in a different manner. If the Minister of Railways will examine Mr. Rogers' report in regard to estimates, he will find that they are lump sums in every instance ; for instance, 175,000 cubic yards for rock excavation, and 5,500,000 exactly for earth excavation. If you follow the estimates all through you will find that they are just lump sums. On the other hand, if you take Mr. Maingy's report or Mr. Rubidge's report, you will find they are figured right down almost to cents. So I think in that regard also there ought to be some inquiry made into that report.
Now, there is another matter which I would like to bring to the attention of the minister, and that is the levels of the great lakes. It seems to me that is one of the most important matters to consider before finally completing this canal. I have taken the trouble to obtain from the Marine Department a chttrt of the lake levels during a large number of years, particularly of Lake Ontario ; and I also have in my possession a chart of the levels of Lakes Michigan and Huron. In examining the one issued by the Marine Department, I find the levels of Lake Ontario almost exactly corresponding in the years I have mentioned. Now, the lake levels have been going down almost steadily since 1838, until in 1895 the Ipwest level was attained by the great lakes that probably ever existed in the history of the country, so far as the memory of man runs, at any rate. In 1895 the level of the great lakes went down about six feet below the level of 1838. In the chart furnished by the Marine Department I find that during the last four years, up to 1901, the level of Lake Ontario has been almost exactly the same, being one and a half foot above the level of 1895, which was the lowest that was ever attained. The low levels of 1899 and 1900 were only six inches above the level of 1895. Now, a gentleman from Port Hope who examined the Trenton harbour last year found that there were only seven feet of water in that harbour, so that if the level of 1895 were to be again attained by Lake Ontario, you would only have

about six feet or six and a half feet of water in the harbour of Trenton. I think the hon. minister knows that the harbour of Trenton has a rocky bottom, and that a great deal of blasting and dredging would have to take place and that in all probability the canal would be perfectly useless if the level of 1895 were to come again. I just call this fact to the attention of the hon. minister because it seems to me that it is a very important thing ; if he does grant this survey, and I think he has given us a good deal of encouragement in that direction, that the lake levels should be taken and that the harbour of Trenton should be most carefully examined. At Port Hope we have a harbour with about fourteen feet of water-perhaps not that depth all through the harbour, but there is a depth of from twelve to fourteen feet all through the harbour. It seems to me that, taking all these things into consideration, we are asking very little in requesting that this comparative survey should be made, and I trust the hon. minister will take it into his most serious consideration and do what I at least think is manifestly in the interests of the country.

Mr. Speaker, the question of the construction of the Trent Valley canal is one of very great interest to the county of Simcoe and to the different counties that abut and adjoin Lake Simcoe. I am not particularly concerned from a local point of view as to whether this canal shall be built, by way of the route suggested by the hon. member for East Durham (Mr. Ward), or whether it shall follow what has in the past been discussed as the probable route, namely by way of Trenton, but, what we wish to see, in the county of Simcoe, is the work speedily taken up and pressed with greater dispatch than it has been since its commencement. I think in this House a great deal of prejudice has been engendered against this work owing to the fact that hon. gentlemen are not conversant with the details of it and I think ifc is to be regretted that the people of Peterborough and those living along that portion of the route where work has been done to a considerable extent have not interested themselves in having other hon. members of this House to go over the route as the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals did a few years ago, and become thoroughly conversant with the wants cf these localities and see how they will be met by the construction of this canal. This system of waterways, extending from Lake Ontario to the waters of Lake Huron, is some 200 miles in length and of this great distance of 200 miles, as I understand, some fifteen or twenty? miles only call for what might be termed, actual canal wbrk. Along the line of the work there are very many large lakes, one of which is Lake Sini-coe. Then, above Peterborough there i^ Stony lake, Pigeon lake and other lakes, the names of which I have not, on the tip Mr. WARD.
of my tongue at the present moment, but I know from having been on them that they are also waters of considerable size. One protest that has been made against the expenditure of money on this canal has been based upon the fact that the boats that would ply on it would be too small to be successful from a business point of view, i may say that the report of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, containing the report of the engineer who is in charge of the work, proves that there is, to-day, over the sills, a depth of six feet of water and when it is considered that boats built with fiat bottoms and having a depth of six feet will carry from 20,000 to 25,000 bushels of grain it must be plain that it would be a considerable factor in the carrying trade of the country. I know that a few years ago an American company that had the choice of erecting an elevator at Buffalo or at a Canadian point, erected an elevator at the town of Midland, where I reside, having a capacity of a million and a quarter bushels and one of the most modern elevators on the great lakes. As a proof of this I may say that it elevates 20,000 bushels per hour which is a fair indication that it must be a very modern concern. I have it from gentlemen interested in the erection of that elevator that one fact that induced them to place their business at Midland was that they would ultimately have water competition from Midland to Montreal. We have spent an immense amount of money on our canal system, and while I am not going to say a word against the amount of money that has been spent on the St. Lawrence canal system, it must be remembered that this Trent Valley canal will be a great feeder to and factor in the St. Lawrence canal system, because, whether the outlet on Lake Ontaro shall be at Trenton or Port Hope, the ultimate destination of the grain carried in vessels will be the port of Montreal. Now, let us look at what has been the effect already of the construction of the locks that have been completed so far. I find from the report of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals last year that no less than 5,185 lockages were made by vessels doing business on these upper lakes. It must be remembered that so far they have not yet had the advantage of being able to go out on Lake Huron or Lake Ontario and that therefore no through trade has been done. Yet, these figures show an increase of 857 lockages over the preceding year. I may say that the hon. minister, when lie went up there a few years ago, and I had the pleasure of being present when he was on that trip, we were surprised to find the class of boats engaged in the trade on the system because there are steamers plying in those waters that will accommodate as many as 400 passengers. It therefore goes without saying that if these locks can accommodate boats of that size, they can also accommodate vessels carrying a considerable amount. of grain.

As a local work for the counties of Simcoe, York and Ontario, it will be of great interest, and let me, in passing, refer to one fact. I am informed that the large cereal concern which has been established at Peterborough was to a certain extent attracted there owing to the fact that it has that magnificent water route which will ultimately give it connection with the waters of the Georgian bay and enable it to bring the vast quantities of grain that it consumes from the upper lake ports to Peterborough and when I say that at that point this one concern is consuming no less than
15,000	bushels of grain per day, and that the expectation is that it will double that in a few years, the importance of this work will be appreciated.
What amount did the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) say it was consuming ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright).

speechtext:
Fifteen thousand bushels a day, and it is estimated that with its capacity it will consume in a very short time no less than 30,000 bushels per day.
On the basis of 30,000 bushels a day, the aggregate would be 10,000,000 a year, which gives a very considerable amount. At present the bulk of that grain is being brought from different points in Ontario, and I know that in the towns of Barrie and Orillia they are purchasing quite a lot of grain and carrying it down by rail. If the canal were constructed they would bring that grain by barges through to Lake Simcoe and the farmers would get the benefit of the decreased rate of transport by water route. At Peterborough there has been established a very large cement concern, and I am told that in establishing these works at Peterborough the company anticipated the construction of this canal. Last year some 15,000,000 bushels of grain arrived at Midland and let me ask, what would it mean to the carrying trade of the whole Dominion if the canal were constructed clear through to Lake Huron ? It would mean that at Midland they would have the benefit of competition between the canal and the railways, and instead of having two large elevators at Midland other elevators would be erected to the great benefit of that town and district. There has been a great deal of delay in the work on this canal. I notice from the report of the Minister of Railways and Canals page 168 that some of these sections have not been dealt with in a very energetic or businesslike manner. The report says
Section 2, Peterborough-Lakefield Division.- The contract for this section was awarded to Messrs. Corry & Laverdure on May 2t, 1896, and the time for completion was November 1, 1897, nearly five years ago. As I reported last year that from the mode of operation adopted by this firm it is difficult to say when the work will be completed. There was only about a month's work to be done by an ordinary force of men at the beginning of this season, but at
the present date it will'still take three months or more to complete the work at the present rate of progress. There is still a considerable amount of concrete to do in connection with the hydraulic lock, as well as excavation in the prism of the canal below the hydraulic lock ; finishing up the sodding, protection lining,
trimming slopes, &c	
The steel work of this hydraulic lock (No.
1, Peterborough) was awarded to the Dominion Bridge Company. Owing to the delay caused by the contractors for the concrete work of the lock not being completed no steel work (except some of that which is to be embedded) has been put in place. A rigid inspection of the main hydraulic presses by tests have been gone on with for some months. Considerable trouble^was experienced in getting the cast iron ram sections cast of the proper consistency and compactness, but this was finally accomplished. Nearly ail the steel work has been prepared and stored on a lot adjoining the bridge works, which has been leased to the government for that purpose.
During this summer while passing along there, I have noticed that the work was much further advanced than last year, and I am told that probably by the first of September the large steel lock will be in running order. When that section is completed boats will be able to go from Balsam lake clear through to Heely's Falls, a distance of about 130 miles. Another feature, and not an unimportant one, of the completion of this canal, is, that it will make that district probably one of the most frequented tourist resorts on the continent of America. At first sight it may not look a business proposition to spend government money for the purpose of improving the facilities for tourist travel, and if that were the only object I would not commend it. At the same time those who live in districts which are frequented by tourists from year to year, know what a profitable trade results. One has but to look at the Thousand Island resorts to see that. In the district of Muskoka, which is not by any means a fertile district, no less than 20,000 people annually visit the beautiful lakes that abound in that region, and these tourists being transient and the number being constantly replaced during the season by others, there is in consequence an enormous outlay of money for the advantage of the proprietors of hotels and of steamboats, as well as the farmers who sell their products for the supplying of these tourists. I would point out to the minister that the different counties that adjoin Lake Simcoe arc. greatly interested in this work, particularly in view of the fact that this large concern at Peterborough to which I have referred uses a great deal of grain, and if the farmers had the opportunity of shipping to Peterborough by water it would be of considerable benefit to them. But the great benefit this canal will confer on the Dominion at large, is that it will be an important feeder to the St. Lawrence canal system. Millions of bushels of grain would be shipped by this route. At the present time the merchants and shippers in Barrie,

Orillia, and other towns have only one competing line to ship over on that division of the Grand Trunk Railway. The section of the Trent canal which is now under contract from Balsam lake to Lake 'Simcoe, has apparently not progressed with much celerity in the past. I understand that the construction of the high level bridge at the crossing of the Midland railway division of the Grand Trunk Railway near Gamebridge has been undertaken by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The work of filling in has been going on pretty fast during the spring and winter and I have noticed that the contractors have a dredge on the ground which I assume will facilitate the work. I would point out to the minister that all along this system of lakes and rivers the movement of freight will be fairly rapid, because I am informed by those who profess to be conversant with it, that three or four of these barges each carrying from 20,000 bushels can, with the aid of powerful tugs, be moved at the rate of six miles an hour. That will be a great improvement over the locomotion in vogue on the Erie canal, and the evidence goes to show that the Erie canal has been a great factor in reducing the rates between New York and Buffalo, and that it has had the effect of compelling the railways to carry freight at a much cheaper rate than they otherwise would. X hope that during the present summer the minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) will press to a conclusion the contract for the section between Balsam lake and Lake Simcoe. I understand that the lock at Kirk-field is similar to the hydraulic lock near Peterborough, and in regard to the lock at Lakefleld I trust that the work will be proceeded with more expeditiously than at other points. Perhaps, when the minister replies, to the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Ward) he will let us know as to the prospect of an early completion of the work at the different points to which I have referred. With reference to the motion made by my hon. friend from East Durham, I can only say that while we in the county of Simcoe are not greatly concerned which route shall be adopted, whether the outlet shall be by Port Hope or by Trenton, we are concerned in this, that there should be a rapid completion of the work connecting the waters of Lake Huron with the waters of Lake Ontario. When the work is completed, and it is bound to be, in view of the money already expended, and in view of the fact that the minister looks with a kindly eye upon it, we should have the satisfaction of seeing vessels carrying from 20,000 to 30,000 bushels of grain loaded at Midland and passing through this canal and in due course to Montreal.
I have noticed this year, what has been most annoying to me as a Canadian, and must be equally so to other gentlemen, that day after day large vessels have been leaving Port William and Port Arthur and going to Buffalo. That means that American vessels,

American lines of railway, and American steamship companies are to-day carrying Canadian grain from the North-west; and it is due to the fact that when the grain arrives at Buffalo, it has not only the advantage of competing lines of railway going to New York, but the additional advantage that they are kept in check by what I must call the almost obsolete system of the Erie canal. Yet that system will not be able to compete with the Trent Valley canal system, either as to the size of vessels or as to cheapness of carriage. I hope to hear from the minister that these works which I have referred to will be proceeded with more rapidly than in the past, and that we should have the satisfaction of seeing an early completion of this important work.

Those of us who have been advocating a speedy construction of the Trent canal for a number of years are delighted to find such places as Port Hope, represented by my bon. friend from East Durham (Mr. Ward), and other important places on Lake Ontario, entering into competition to secure the terminus of the canal. We had a somewhat uphill fight for some years to convince the hon. members of this House of the advantages of this canal, not only to the localities through which it passes, but to the whole of Canada. That day, Sir, has happily gone by. We now find our good friend the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) thoroughly impressed with the necessity of pushing the construction of this canal to a speedy completion ; and not a voice is raised on either side of the House in opposition to the construction of this great work. The hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has ably placed before the Plouse and the country many of its advantages ; but X may lie permitted to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to this fact as an incentive to hasten its completion. At present the farmers of western Iowa can land their grain in T.iverpool at five or six cents a bushel less than the farmers of the Midland district of Ontario, owing to the difference in freight rates, by reason of the water route from Chicago to the seaboard via the Erie canal, keeping down the rates on the railways. I can assure Hie Minister of Railways and Canals that when the Trent canal is completed, if in the immediate future we will erect monuments to him and his predecessor.
One'will be enough.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do not mean post mortem monuments ; but we will put up tablets in his honour all along the route of the canal, for pushing it through to speedy completion, and increasing the value of the grains raised by the farmers of that district at least five cents a bushel. We have a number of important towns along the route of the

canal. Bordering- on Lake Simcoe we have the magnificent towns of Barrie, Orillia and Beaverton, all of wliicli will be greatly benefited by being provided with communication with tbe outer world. Passing on, we come to the village of Kirkfield, the village of Fenelou Falls, and tbe town of Lindsay, in tlie county of Victoria, and the fine little town of Port Perry, in tbe county of Ontario. Then, in tbe county of Peterborough, we come to tbe village of Lakefield and tbe town of Peterborough, and in tbe county of Northumberland, tbe village of Canip-bellford. All these towns would be greatly benefited by the construction of this canal. Then, there are many water powers along tbe route of tbe canal, which would bring in new industries now unthought of. It has been very properly stated that this is not a canal In the ordinary sense of the term, but rather a series of inland lakes connected by locks. Beginning at Midland, there is a cutting of a few miles to Lake Couclii-ching, where we have open water across Lake Simcoe. From Lake Simcoe the route is already under construction ty the Talbot river to Balsam lake, with little cutting, and one hydraulic lock at Kirkfield. Across Balsam lake we have a stretch of open water for about eight miles to Cameron lake ; and across Cameron lake for three miles brings us to Fenelou Falls. There are two locks already constructed connecting Cameron lake to Sturgeon lake, through a river about half a mile long. Across Sturgeon lake there is open water for twelve miles to Bobcaygeon, where a lock is already constructed. Then we come to short river about half a mile in length, with rocky banks, so that the speed of vessels need not be retarded. This brings us to Pigeon lake, where we have another stretch of open water for about twelve miles through Buckhorn lake. Here there is a lock already constructed in a rocky cutting leading to Deer lake and Lovesick lake. Thence, by two locks at Burleigh, we come to Stony lake ; and through Stony lake we have open water for five miles, until we enter the navigable waters of the Otonabee river, connecting, by a magnificent hydraulic lift-lock at Peterborough, with the waters of the lower Otonabee and Rice lake.
My hon. friend from Bast Durham (Mr. Ward), I regret to say, seems to consider that Mr. Rogers has given a report to the minister which is not based on most reliable data, in that opinion I am satisfied my hon. friend is entirely mistaken. I am convinced that any report which Mr. Rogers would give will be found absolutely correct. Following the Trent river route, which is the natural waterway, it will be found that the main difference between the estimates of Mr. Rubidge and Mr. Rogers consists in the fact that Mr. Rogers proposed following the waterway itself, damming the river and utilizing its shores for locks, while Mr. Rubidge intended to cut the canal right
through the solid rock all the way. Mr. Rogers' proposition is that the waterway itself should be utilized and locks should be built here and there at the end of the dams, as they might be required. My personal sympathies would all lie in favour of the Port Hope route, and I would be very pleased if its advantages were such as to commend that route for adoption, but while my hon. friend points out that it is fifty miles from the mouth of the Otonabee river to Trenton by the river way and only nineteen miles to Port Hope, he leaves out of consideration the fact that it is thirty miles from Port Hope to Trenton, and that at least twenty-six of these are along the open waters of Lake Ontario, where you would be storm-tossed by every wind on the lake. That, however, is a matter of detail, which I am satisfied will be settled by the engineers. I shall not dwell at length on this proposition, but confine myself to stating that from the point of view of the benefit to the counties through which this canal will pass, it cannot be equalled by the construction of any railway that could be proposed, and for the benefit to the Dominion, as a through route for the output of the grain of the North-west, it would save a distance of three hundred miles as compared with the route away round by the river Detroit. In this respect it should commend itself to shippers. No doubt it has to meet the opposition of shippers who already have their lake barges constructed to ply between Kingston aim Montreal. The Montreal Transportation Company do not favour this project because their steam barges are constructed for the purpose of navigating the Welland canal, but there is ample freight for all our western and eastern ports.
They are going to Buffalo now.

Yes. Even when this canal is constructed there will still be ample employment for these enormous barges, each carrying from 200,000 to
250,000	bushels of grain from Tort Arthur to Fort William and even from Duluth and Chicago. Even by this canal the barges could transport that grain right to the city of Montreal. The same barges that load the grain at Midland could carry it without breaking bulk, directly to Slontreal. It is a fallacious notion to my mind-it lias been so proven by the best engineers-that canals, in order to be successful and profitable should be of enormous depth. We had a fad in Canada a number of years ago, in favour of twenty-one feet canals. That is a very fine theory, but when you consider the enormous cost of constructing such a canal and of constructing the necessary steel barges required on a canal of that depth, and then consider that the return trips will, in all probability, be light, you will find that the most profitable canal-the one that will carry the greatest quantity of grain barges and any class of freight at good prices-is the average canal. Why the Erie

canal liad a depth of only four and a half feet on the sills and has not yet much improved on that. Yet that canal has built up immense cities all along its route and proved of such value to the farmers and business men of the state of New York that they would not sacrifice it for the enormous sum of $30,000,000. Although the railway companies have made all sorts of efforts to obtain control of that canal and remove it as a competitor, the people of the state of New York will not give it up and are taxing themselves annually enormous sums to preserve its integrity. Until recent years, it was only four and 'a half feet deep and eighteen feet wide. Now, the Trent canal will have a depth of eight feet of water on the sills and will carry barges capable of carrying from twenty-five to thirty thousand bushels of grain each over its entire route. A steamer from Midland harbour, carrying 250,000 bushels of grain, could unload its cargo in! ten barges which could be towed down to Montreal, without any trouble, by one or two tugs. It is not necessary that any argument to point out the necessity of building this canal should be advanced. Our only desire is to urge on the Minister of Railways and Canals, the necessity for the immediate completion of this great work. I know that his mind is now thoroughly seized with its advantages. It would be good enough to put in the supplementary estimates, a sum which would complete the route between Lake Couchich-ing and Midland harbour, in order that hi another year there may be ingress to and egress from the waters of the western lakes, and in another year put in a sum to complete it to Tort Hope, I am satisfied that he wouid confer on the Dominion in general, and the province of Ontario in particular,
* one of the greatest benefits that can be imagined.

I have no objection at all to offer to the passing of the motion moved by my hon. friend from East Durham (Mr. Ward), provided it be passed subject to the understanding that we shall only bring down such papers, reports and documents bearing on the subject as have not already been laid before parliament. My hon. friend is naturally interested in the particular locality lie represents and anxious that when a final selection of the route be made for the outlet of this canal into Lake Ontario, Port Hope may be the one chosen. And in urging upon the department and the House his conviction that Port Hope is the proper point, my hon. friend is only discharging his duty to his constituents. But I am not sure that he has done quite justice to the engineer of the department in the criticism he has cast on that engineer's report. If I understood him correctly, he pointed out that Mr. Rogers, the engineer, had made a very much larger estimate of the quantity of earth excavation than Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
would be required than had been previously made by the engineer who first made the survey. I think he said that Mr. Rogers' estimate was something over five million, while the other was not much in excess of two million. I think the hon. gentleman had not present in his mind the fact that the locks which would be required along that work are very much larger indeed than were contemplated when the first survey took place. The first lock was seventy feet in length, thirteen feet in width and four feet in depth. The present lock would be one hundred and thirty three feet in length, thirty-three feet in width and six feet in depth.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: With a possibility of eight feet.

I do not say that. I am speaking of the engineer's estimate, and his calculation was based on six feet. But the hon. gentleman can see that there is room for probably all the difference he pointed out and because of which he criticised the report of the engineer. I cannot say that the engineer may not have a preference in his own mind for the Trenton over the Port Hope location, but I think it would not be fair to assume that such judgment is based upon other than a conviction reached after proper inquiry. He may or may not be right. Other engineers may or may not agree with him. Still, all parties who may have made different reports may have reached their conclusions after exercising their best judgment and brought honest minds to bear upon the problem. I do know, however, Mr. Speaker, that there is admittedly some considerable difference between what would be the probable cost of construction by the Port Hope route and to the cost of construction by the Trenton route. But there has always been the objection raised by the officers of my department, that after getting to the lake, you are obliged to travel a considerable distance-some forty odd miles-along a very exposed shore of the lake, with these small barges.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
May I correct the hon. gentleman ?
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. I speak now,	of course, of barges
going to Montreal.

May I correct the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) on one point ?
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. Certainly.

It is only twenty-six miles to the Murray canal-that is, to the headland going into the Murray canal-from Port Hope-not forty miles.
The	MINISTER	OF	RAILWAYS	AND
CANALS. The fact that there is a further
distance before you get to the islands is a fact that cannot be ignored. There is

exposure there, and this onght to be considered in the opinion ot some of our engineers. They do. regard it seriously, and it is a fact that has to be allowed for in determining which of these two routes should be chosen. I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Ward) that a delegation waited upon me in the department some weeks ago, and after I had heard, I must confess, a very businesslike presentation of the whole case from these gentlemen, I felt it was my duty to consider it. I have been led to the conclusion that an officer of the department should be sent, separate from any who have heretofore gone, and I have already made the selection of the officer, and he lias instructions to make this survey, a survey that will cover not only the Port Hope route but the other, so that the judgment of the engineer who made the one survey may be applied to the other as well. So, I hope my hon. friend will feel that the question he urges upon us has not been overlooked.
My hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has glanced at the subject generally but has made particular reference to the progress of the work now under contract, and has asked me to indicate, if I could, how soon these works will he brought to a conclusion. I may say that I did not supply myself with data as fully as I should have done this afternoon if I had known that the whole subject of the Trent valley canal was coming up in this debate. But I am in a position to say that, while the works have not been prosecuted by the contractors as speedily as we would have desired, and as we expected, I think there is some justification and excuse for the delay. 1 am quite certain that the works remaining to be finished will be carried forward with all possible despatch. My hon. friend intimated that it was two years since I visited the canal. I made it my business to pass along thel route of that portion of the canal where works were in 'progress last fall, and I saw the contractors who were working and heard their explanations as to the delay. I am bound to say there was some excuse for the delay. But X have been given to understand very positively that so far as the Brown & Aymer contract is concerned that the work to Lake Simcoe, will be done this fall. As to the other part, the only thing that remains to be completed is the hydraulic lift. We are pushing that forward, I think, with a great deal of despatch, and we hope that, inside of a couple of months, we shall have the lift in operation. We think it necessary to have that lift in operation before we enter into a contract for the erection of the second-in fact, before we make any plans of too definite a character. There may lie some improvements which will be suggested by the actual operation of the lock. The hydraulic lift is a new thing in Canada. I understand there are only two or three in operation anywhere. We hope to have the one at Peterborough in such shape that it can be tested and ready for operation inside of two months. Then, if its operation is generally satisfactory, we shall be in a position to call for tenders for the one at Kirkfield, and we will do so without any delay. The completion of the work through to Lake Huron will involve quite a little expenditure of money. My hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) appeals to me to ask for money and have this work prosecuted, I would like him to give us credit, which we are certainly entitled to, of having carried the work on with a moderate degree of despatch, at all events, as compared with the methods adopted by our predecessors.
Oh, oh.

Yes, we have spent a great deal of money every year, more than was spent previous to the advent of the present government to power. Money we spend very reluctantly, and always in fear that the volume of our expenditure will be criticised by our friends in opposition. When an appropriation is asked the government have to have in mind that hon. gentlemen on the other side will add all these sums together and will claim that our outlay, capital and consolidated, should be lumped together and that these large figures should be presented to the country as showing how extravagant and wasteful we are and how utterly indifferent to the adoption of economical methods.
Now we must have all these things present in our minds. My hon. friends, if they do not succeed in doing anything else, may succeed in alarming us by their strictures for making these large outlays. Now, having all these things in mind, seeing that we have done so well in the past, and that we are struggling along moderately well at present, I hopes my hon. friends will not press us too strongly to make too large expenditures in the future. I shall be glad to see the work go on with the customary speed. When it is completed, I think that, though it may not in some respects fulfil all expectations which have been formed by some hon. gentlemen opposite, still I am satisfied that it will turn out to be useful, and will prove valuable to the locality through which it passes. 1 agree with the hon. member for East {31m-coe (Mr. Bennett) that a more attractive, a more charming section of the country for tourists could not possibly be found than that which will be traversed by this canal.
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I hope the conscience of the Minister of Railways and Canals will not check him any more in any other expenditure he makes, than it does on this expenditure on that Trent canal.

Allow me to say, as one who visited the town of

Peterborough and vicinity lasts year, that I had occasion, with some of the citizens of the town, to examine the lift loch and to hear a great deal about this canal. From the information which I gathered I became convinced that the completion of this canal will not only be very useful to the locality through which it passes, but it is likely to become an important feeder to the trade of Montreal. Taking that view of it, I wish to say that so far as we are concerned in the east, we will be ready at any time to vote the necessary money for the completion of that great and important waterway. I am sorry to hear the Minister of Railways and Canals express so much fear of the criticism which might result from that expenditure. We are always ready to approve an expenditure of that kind made in a proper manner. During the election in Maisonneuve a short time ago, I heard the Minister of Marine and Fisheries tell us positively on many occasions that the whole question of transportation, (o use his own expression, from the Yukon to the Atlantic Ocean, was going to be placed under his immediate control and taken out of the other departments. When I heard this declaration I felt the greatest confidence that the qualms of conscience which are moving the minister would not appear in the case of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries who was then coming forward for election.

Perhaps it would be only right for me to say, in view of the fact that I have always opposed this work, that I have changed my mind since I have had an opportunity lately' of examining a portion of the canal and ascertaining more about the local conditions, and the value of it, than I have heretofore known. My judgment of the canal now is that it will be a much more valuable highway of commerce than I was ever inclined to give it credit for. It is true that the depth is not great, and is not intended to be, when it is completed. That is the reason why I always supposed that it could not be much of a highway for the purpose of carrying through freight or grain. I still think that as a through line it will not be of any great use in carrying grain, for instance, to Montreal or other eastern markets, because I think that the transhipments in two different places will increase too much the cost of carriage, and it might be carried a much greater distance around without transshipment at about the same cost. But it will be a valuable highway of commerce, for the locality in bringing in grain which could not otherwise be brought in. I need only refer to the one industry at Peterborough, which is to my mind of great importance to the country, that is, the cereal food mill they have established there, and which is destined to use a large amount of grain when running to its fullest capacity, Mr. MONK.
which it cannot do to-day on account of the inconvenience in bringing in grain. I was told by' the manager of this mill that when running at its fullest capacity they would use 10,000,000 to 13,000,000 bushels of grain per year, and they could even increase it to 30,000,000 bushels of grain yearly if they had the convenience which they ought to have to bring in grain and tranship the products with the greatest facility and at the least cost. That is only one of many establishments along the route of that canal that would be served if the canal was finished, as it ought to be. Now the fact that Ontario does not supply the grain required for the needs of this establishment, a large portion of it must come from the North-west. As it comes down the lakes and reaches the nearest port on the lake, there is only; one transhipment before it gets to the mill. At the mill it must be unloaded and manufactured there, and of course the products must be reloaded again. Whether the wheat is being converted into flour, or whether the wheat, oats or barley are being. converted into the other cereal foods that the institution is intended to manufacture, the grain must come largely from the North-west. It has to be laid down there and manufactured and transhipped, and to do that cheaply this canal is very much required; and until it is finished these industries are much hampered in carrying on their important operations. I have always opposed it because of the heavy expenditure; but I believe there would be a compensation and a return for that expenditure. I believe the country' would be amply justified in making the expenditure at an early date because we cannot get these industries established a moment too soon, othewise trade will drift into other channels.
There is to my mind another important advantage which will accrue from the completion of that canal. All the heavy lines of goods, the metal lines, such as nails and machinery of every kind that are taken from Montreal westward, could be carried through that canal much cheaper than they could be carried by' railway. The canaj will not only be a. valuable highway for the various towns along the route of the canal, and on the Georgian bay as well, but it will be a great aid in keeping down the freight rates of the railways. If it was built at the present time it would reduce the freight rates on the railways to those inland towns to a very large extent, and the saving upou the cost of freight would be an important item, not only to the people handling the goods and to those establishments that are manufacturing grain as well, but to the consumers in the locality where these goods must be used. Another respect in which I think it will be valuable is in that it. furnishes us with an example of the utility of these lift locks. Although that may not be a new invention in Canada, it has

hitherto been an untried thing in Canada, and it seems to me that this lift-loek at Peterborough is going to solve many important canal questions for Canada. It seems to me that it will work all right and if you can lift a vessel forty-five feet you can just as well lift it sixty-five, or seventy feet. We ought to have it tried to ascertain whether it will do all we expect or not, so that we will knowi whether it can be used on other routes as well. For these reasons I am in favour of finishing that caual. I think the government would be amply justified in making the expenditure necessary to finish it and I for one feel that they would be doing a good work not only for the locality but for the country generally by the expenditure of money for the purpose of finishing it.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to say that I regret very much if I went beyond the limits of fair criticism in speaking of Mr. Rogers' report. I had no intention of doing so, but I simply referred to it to compare his estimate with the different estimates contained in Mr. Rubidge's report which is the only one we can compare it with. Mr. Rubidge's report, as you well know, recommended a five foot canal and Mr. Rogers' report upon the Port Hope canal was for a six foot canal. That should be taken into consideration also. In so far as the large quantity of earth excavation is concerned which the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) referred to-rlie lost sight of the fact that the greater part of that excavation was going through the height of land. It was not in taking out the earth for the locks, but the greater portion of it was going through the height of land. You must bear in mind also that Mr. Rogers estimated that the level of the land with the lake was 4J miles from the lake instead of 2i or 3 miles as in Mr. Maingy's report, and I know as a matter of fact, that the land dips from the level of the lake again about 3 miles from Rice lake. Therefore, I think there is some ground for tlie criticism I made. It is simply a matter of figures and I had no idea whatever of reflecting upon Mr. Rogers. In regard to the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes), he has presented the argument of the Peterborough people, the sole argument, I think, used by the opposition which has taken place since we have been advocating the Port Hope route. That is the open lake argument. Perhaps my hon. friend is not aware that from Cleveland, barges constantly go down to the mouth of the Brie canal at Buffalo, 100 miles, whereas, there is only open lake, as far as this end of the Trent valley canal is concerned, from Port Hope to the headland going through the entrance of the Murray canal, a distance of 26 miles.

Would my hon. friend (Mr. Ward) allow me to say that I
entered into no discussion whatever of the merits of the two routes.

Still, the hon. gentleman uses that argument. It is the stock argument of the opponents of the Port Hope route. The open lake should not make any great difference and for this reason :	I have
been informed by mariners who have been all their lives on Lake Ontario that they would very much prefer going down by the open lake from the outlet of the canal, to going down by way of the Bay of Quints. That is a matter in regard to which I have been spoken to on several occasions by different captains of vessels. Now, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals lias referred also to the deep waterway, and it seems to me that in view of the fact that at no very distant day Canada will require a deeper waterway than five or six feet, it will be well for the government before going on and filling these two gaps in the canal to consider whether it would not be wise to make the canal eight feet at once instead of six feet. In regard to that I have also the evidence of some shippers at Kingston, who tell me that the 8,000 bushel barges which would lie the capacity of barges going through a five foot canal could not possibly go down the St. Lawrence and pay. They would have to tranship at Kingston in any event and the grain or whatever cargo they carried would have to be placed in larger barges. There is a freight rate of one and five-eighths cents a bushel from Kingston to Montreal and it would be very much cheaper to tranship at Kingston than to send these small barges down the St. Lawrence. If a deep waterway were constructed and vessels of the capacity of an eight foot canal were to go down it would be quite easy for these large barges to come from Kingston to Port Hope and tranship there ; in fact, they could do that even if only 8,000 bushel barges were used. I do not think, therefore, that the open lake argument is one which can be used against the completion of the canal by way of Port Hope.. I would therefore urge upon the hon. minister again that the matter of the water levels of the great, lakes ought to be taken into consideration before anything is done and that the harbour of Trenton ought to be carefully surveyed so that it can be seen, whether, as a matter of fact, if the level of the water went down to the point reached in 1895, it would absolutely shut up the canal for the time during which the water remained at that level.

Mr. Speaker, there does not appear to be any serious difference of opinion in regard to the advisability of the construction of tills waterway. This is a matter which had its inception with the Conservative party I in power before the present government
Might I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Porter) to what particular appropriation he refers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I cannot give you the exact figure, Sir, but in looking over the appropriations from year to year, I notice that $300,000 has been appropriated for the Trent valley canal, and that the expenditure has been far below that amount. It appears to me that if it were necessary to appropriate that amount, it should be necessary to expend it.
Whether you could properly expend it or not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: At all events, I find that in the year preceding a general election both the appropriation and the expenditure is largely increased, and that I complain of.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Porter) is very anxious apparently that the canal should proceed slowly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am very anxious to have the canal constructed, because I believe it to be a work of very great benefit to the country at large. I do not think it is of any advantage to this country to have the government trifling with this matter as they have been trifling with it. In conclusion, Sir, I again strongly urge upon the government the importance of determining at an early date, the route of this canal. And I trust that in the interest of the country they will see that it is completed as soon as possible.
