Mr. ARCHIBALD CAMPBELL (West York) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 20) to amend the Weights and Measures Act. He said :	The object of this Bill
is to provide an authorized can for the sale of milk in the towns and cities throughout the Dominion. As is well known milk is sold by the can throughout the Dominion. In Ontario, it is an understood rule that eight gallons should constitute a can of milk, and the custom has been for the farmers to contract with the dealers in the cities or towns for one, two or three cans as they may be able to supply. The dealers, as a rule, furnish the cans, and, as there is no law to define how many gallons a can of milk shall hold, it has become a practice to make the cans a little larger and a little larger, until, at the present time, there are hardly any cans in use in Ontario that hold less than from eight and a half to nine gallons. The farmers are obliged to fill the cans, otherwise they will be docked. Thus you will see that the farmers are furnishing from one-half to two-thirds of a gallon of milk for every can more than they should and more than they get paid for. This may seem a small thing, but when you recollect that, in Toronto alone, it is estimated that three thousand

cans of milk are brought in every day, this extra quantity of from one-half to two-thirds of a gallon becomes a serious thing indeed for the farmer. They have complained a good while about this injustice, but without steps having been taken to remove the grievance. Last session, I had the honour of introducing a Bill upon the subject, but it was too late and could not go through that session. So, I have reintroduced the measure this year. This Sill does no injustice to anybody. It does not interfere with the present cans' or with any cans. One may make cans to hold eight or ten gallons or any quantity he likes; all that the Bill provides is that when a farmer sells a can of milk it shall mean that he sells eight gallons. In the province of Quebec this Bill has met with great favour also. I have a letter from Mr. Robert Ness, President of the Milk Shippers' Association. He says ;
Howiclc, April 2, 1903. Archibald Campbell, Esq., M.P.
Dear Sir,-Your favour of 1st duly received and noted. I am very pleased to see you have taken up this question. Our people have spoken quite often of the tendency of the milk vendors to increase the size of the can. Some of them have even refused taking it if the can is not filled. In most cases the can holds jnore than the measure. I am certain the association of which I have the honour to be president will heartily approve of your Bill on every point. I hope you will succeed in getting it made law. If we agree to supply so many gallons of milk, the right measure is all that should be required. If we can assist you in any way don't be backward in asking us. Thanking you for favour.
I am yours,

President Milk Shippers' Association, Montreal, Que.
I sent Mr. Ness a copy of the Bill and asked him for his approval. I am sure that this is a Bill that should receive no opposition, for it only provides in the case of milk what is provided in the case of other commodities. In every other commodity, parliament has settled what shall be meant by certain terms. For instance, if you sell a man a bag of potatoes, the law says that ninety pounds must be furnished. I see that in the province of Quebec, if you sell a bundle of hay or straw, timothy hay or clover hay, the law says how many pounds shall be in the bundle. If you sell a barrel of flour or a barrel of salt, or a bushel of wheat, or oats, or barley, or peas, the law says just how many pounds you shall furnish. Here is a commodity that has been sold for many years, the sale of which is a matter of great interest to the farmers, not only in the province of Ontario, but in every other province, but there is no law to determine what the measure shall be. So 1 hope the Bill will meet with the approval of the House. The Bill is very brief. The first section provides :

When milk is sold by the can, the can shall be considered as equivalent to eight gallons, and the half can to four gallons.
This does not interfere with tlic package at all. As I say, the can may be made to hold any quantity. The Bill merely provides that when a man has contracted to deliver a can of milk, the delivery of eight gallons shall fill that contract, or, half a can, four gallons. The second section reads :
Milk cans shall, when presented for verification to any inspector of weights and measures, be inspected and stamped with their capacity as then determined.
And, for this there is a fee, provided for as follows :
The Governor in Council may make a tariff of fees to be paid for inspecting and stamping milk cans, but the said fees shall not exceed one and one-half cent per gallon.
1 move the second reading of this Bill.

Id. KEMP (East Toronto). I would inquire of the Minister of Inland Revenue, (Hon. Mr. Bernier) before I speak on this Bill, if the government! intend to take this matter up. I understood the hon. minister intended to look into this Bill and see what had better be done.

As I understand the Bill, it is proposed as an amendment to the Weights and Measures Act. It has no reference to the affairs under my department, unless parliament designs to adopt a new standard. This Bill provides that when milk shall be sold by the can, the can shall be considered as equivalent to eight gallons, and half a can to four gallons. The law now recognizes as measures of capacity the following :	Bushel, half-bushel, peck, gallon,
half-gallon, quart, pint, half-pint, gill, and half-gill. The Bill proposes to add another measure which shall be equivalent to eight gallons. That is to say a certain can shall be manufactured supposed to contain eight gallons, or half a can four gallons. I wonder how that plan will work unless the vendor and purchaser agree to accept these measures. The Bill, as I read it, does not make that can a standard measure, but a substitute for it. Under these circumstances, I do not think my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) will reach his object unless parliament creates a new standard. If that new standard is created, all my department will have to do will be to inspect the new measures of capacity. I have considered, as I have already informed my hon. friend, that this Bill relates to matters coming within the scope of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I will ask him to wait until the Minister of that department (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) is present.
speakername: The MINISTER OF INLAND REVENUE (Hon, M. E. Bernier).

speechtext:
If it is the intention to hold the Bill over I will wait until it comes up for discussion. I presume my hon. friend will be willing to

have it lay over at the request of the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue.
This is the last day we may reach it. If we do not go on with it now, we may as well throw it up for the session. If there are any objections, I think we might hear them now.

If the Bill is laid over at the request of my hon. colleague, the Minister of Inland Revenue, owing to the absence of my hon. colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the government will be obliged to facilitate this discussion later on. It would not be fair to cause it to be laid aside and then shut it out at a later day.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext:
Since the Bill is before the House, it may be as well for us to consider its effects now, even though it may come up again at a later day. I quite approve of fixing a standard for milk cans. That has been ft live question within a radius of Toronto for a number of years, but I am at a loss to interpret the present Bill, and fear that a good deal of trouble might follow, if adopted in its present form. The clause reads :
When milk is sold by the can, the can shall be considered as equivalent to eight gallons and the half can to four gallons.
As I understand this clause, it can make no difference how much milk there is in the can. Whether it contains seven or nine gallons, it is to be considered as equivalent to eight gallons.
The number of gallons will be eight. It would not be a can if it contained anything less.

I fail to see that the Bill states positively that the can must contain eight gallons, neither more nor less. No matter how much milk there may be in tlie can when delivered by the fanner to the dealer, it is to be considered as equivalent to eight gallons, even though the can should contain seven gallons or nine gallons. It seems to me that the Bill is badly worded, and that some change should be made in the wording in order to prevent the possibility of misunderstanding. I do not wish to oppose this Bill, because I think it is of a kind that is called for, and attempts along this line have been made in past years to secure legislation of this character. But if we are to pass legislation at all, we should make it so definite as to avoid any possibility of dispute. In the second clause there is no light thrown upon the first, because under it a can of any size could be inspected and stamped by the inspector of weights and measures. The second clause reads :
Milk cans shall, when presented for verification to any inspector of weights and measures, be inspected and stamped with their capacity as then determined.
74i
A can may be inspected as containing nine gallons or seven gallons. If inspected as a seven gallon can, the purchaser knows that it cannot contain more than seven gallons, but it may contain less,' so that there is no protection to the purchaser. It will be necessary to have a standard can to which, after a lapse of two years, all cans should conform. At present the milk cans are of varied capacity. Some are seven gallon cans and some are eight and more than eight. If the hon. gentleman would provide that after a certain time, sufficient for the present cans to be worn out, only cans of a fixed capacity of eight gallons could be used, this Bill would be more effective. There would then be no dispute possible, as the can would be a standard measure, just the same as a gallon or a half gallon or a quart measure. I do not make these observations for the purpose in any way of hindei'ing the passage of a Bill of this kind, because I know that my own constituents are interested in having such a measure become law, but I would like to have the Bill passed in such a way as to avoid dispute.

I have had several letters from different parties asking me to fin<j out whether this Bill is going to be endorsed by tlie government, or be withdrawn, so that they might know whether it will be necessary for them to come to Ottawa to protest against it. The size of the milk cans now in use vary from two to forty gallons ; and while some of the milk in the country is sold by gallon, the greater portion of it is sold by weight. To the cheese and butter factories it is sold by weight. Those who have spoken to me in opposition to the Bill say that they are willing that a law should be passed providing that the milk be sold by weight, but they protest very strongly against this measure. I hope the hon. gentleman will be willing to let the Bill lay over until the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue has heard these deputations, because a great deal of money has been invested in all these various sized vessels for conveying milk. If a standard can should be adopted that would cause great loss to those who own the cans now in use. In 1892 a measure of this kind was adopted and in 1898 it was cancelled, and a new regulation put into effect. That regulation I have before me. The Minister of Inland Revenue has read from that regulation the standards used for measuring all kinds of liquors. The intention of this Bill is to make another standard, and is impracticable. These cans are carried into the cities by railways and wagons, and after the first trip or two they become indented and their capacity is less. That portion of the present law which was read by the Minister of Inland Revenue provides that:
No measure of capacity, of which the sides or bottoms are indented, battered or knocked out of regular form, will be admitted to verification.

Therefore, if these cans were taken to the inspector to be verified, after they had become dinged, he would refuse to verify them. In other words, the'standards of the country are not to be used for the purpose of conveying commodities, they are to be used in the most careful manner. A man having a measure is supposed to take the greatest care of it and put it in a place where it will not be dinged or indented, in consequence of which the capacity of that measure might become impaired. I think it is impossible to use a measure of this kind for the purpose of conveying any commodity. But if it is absolutely necessary to make a law regulating the sale of all milk, let the law be made to sell it by weight, as is already done in many parts of the country. At any rate, I want to say to the Minister of Inland Revenue that I fully expected an opportunity would be afforded whereby I might be able to notify those who have been opposing the Bill of a date upon which they could wait upon the minister in regard to this matter. Another objection to the Bill is made on account of the excessive fees which would be charged for verification, sixteen cents on every can, and that sixteen cents would be good only so long as the can remained undinted and in its original shape. As I said before, if this Bill becomes law it will cause great loss to those who own cans. One of the largest dealers in milk in Toronto at the present time, who handles one-sixth of the whole product in the city of Toronto, buys its milk by weight, and does not depend altogether upon the size of the can. The seller of milk knows exactly what he is going to get for a certain weight of milk. A gallon of milk, as we know weighs ten pounds, eighty pounds of milk would be eight gallons. There is a measure now recognized on the statute-book, that is called a bushel measure, which contains eight gallons. I trust that the hon. gentleman will yield to the wishes of the Minister of Inland Revenue and leave this matter over until we have more time to consider it.

I do not see why there should be any urgent need for the Bill at all. It seems to me that we are better off now than we would be if the Bill passed. In the event of this Bill becoming law, you would only have two sizes of cans. Now the quantity of milk that a farmer can furnish from day to day varies a good deal. He must either send cans partly filled, or else have more than one can. Why not be able to use any sized can you like, and sell your milk by the gallon ? Let the buyers offer to purchase as they like. The farmer is not obliged to sell execpt by the gallon or as he agrees to. The standard is a gallon, then why not use the standard we have ? There is no farmer who has a number of cans but will find that the quantity of milk he has to sell varies from

day to day, scarcely two days alike, owing to the different kinds of food he gives his cattle, and the many other causes that affect the milk supply. Many farmers always send what they can spare, as many gallons as they can spare. There would be no objection to have all the cans stamped with their capacity, an eight gallon can stamped as a measure that will hold eight gallons, and a four gallon can stamped as a measure that will hold four gallons, and so on. In selling milk by gallons, there can be no injustice done to either the farmer or the purchaser. When that is done, the farmer can use the can that is most convenient for him to use according to the supply of milk he has on hand. On the other hand, if you adopt the other standard of selling milk by the pound, that is perfectly fair to both the buyer and the seller. In that event, there is no need of having any provision as to the size of the can at all; use any can you like, you are selling the milk at so much a pound, the farmer is paid for the number of pounds he delivers, and no more. It seems to me that no farmer can be injured in that way, and the purchaser always knows what he is getting, and what he is paying for. I think we would only be increasing the evil by making another standard, and we would be increasing the inconvenience to the farmer whose quantity of milk that he has to sell varies so much from day to day.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I was going to say to the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) who introduced this Bill, that I would like him to look after the interest of the consumer of milk. This Bill is evidently intended to apply to the seller of milk who sells in large quantities, and to the purchaser of large quantities, or to the consumer who purchases his milk by the can. In our town, and I presume it is the same all over, the milk vendors sell milk by the can or the quart, they deliver a quart can at your door every morning. .
We don't (interfere with that at all.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Certainly, but when the milk is sold by the can the can must be considered an equivalent to eight gallons. Where will my hon. friend provide a can that is equivalent to a quart or two quarts ? That is like what he wanted to do to help the market gardeners; it is merely to make the milk vendors believe that he is going to do something for them. As the Minister of Inland Revenue stated a few moments ago, we have a standard to-day fixing what a can should be. Now a farmer in the country sends in his can of milk to the retailer, who sells to the consumer by the gallon, or by the pound, if he chooses to make a bargain to do so. But he cannot say, this can contains ten gallons, or fifteen gallons, he says :	The can contains so
much. If the purchaser, when he comes to

measure out that can of milk, finds that it does not contain the quantity the farmer sold it for, the latter is liable to a penalty by the old Act. Every person who sells a less quantity than the Act provides for is liable to punishment. Therefore I see no necessity for this Bill at all. It will work injuriously to the seller and the consumer placed on the government orders. I want to ask tl;e Minister of Finance a question, that is drawn out by the hon. gentleman who introduced this Bill. The Minister of Inland Revenue asked that the Bill might lie over until the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in whose department this Bill belongs, would be present. The hon. member who has charge of this Bill says this is the last day that we will have an opportunity of dealing with public bills and orders.
It might be.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And the Minister of Finance said that on account of the government asking that this Bill should lie over, they would see that an opportunity was given to have it brought up, or perhaps placed on the government Orders. I want to ask the Minister of Finance in what position that arrangement will place these Bills that are not printed. I see here a Bill introduced by the hon. member for St. Lawrence, Montreal, (Mr. Bickerdike) in reference to cigarettes, which is not yet printed in English or French. That Bill has not been printed and as this is likely to be the last day for the consideration of public Bills and Orders and as that Bill is nearly at the bottom of the Order Paper it is very liable not to be heard this session if it is not taken under the government's wing. This being the case is it the intention of the government to place the Bill of the hon. member for Montreal (St. Antoine) amongst government orders ?

My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) is hardly correct in stating that this is the last day for the consideration of Public Bills and Orders. It may be that Mondays may be taken, but it has not yet been determined upon, and if there are a number of Bills on the Order Paper which have not then been reached that would be a very fair reason why the government should not take Mondays. I think thq hon. gentleman may very well assume that there will be another opportunity of dealing with those Bills which are on the Order Paper.

Mr. Speaker, I do not profess to know whether or not it would better serve the interests of the milk trade that a further provision such as my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) points to in this Bill should be adopted. However, It does appear to me to be somewhat difficult to set up a standard. If you are going to establish a new standard it must be
a standard which will have a distinct name, and call for a distinct quality. As to whether this is feasible or not, I think the question is of such intricacy that it is one upon which the proper officers of the proper department might very well decide before my hon. friend presses this Bill for further consideration. We would scarcely be in a position to-night to make much progress with a Bill as it stands at present. Then, if it is desirable that a standard measure, to be called a can, shall be legalized, I would take it that my hon. friend would need to change very materially the phraseology of the Bill, because, I quite agree with the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) when he criticised the language of the first clause and pointed out that the use of the words which says that a can shall be equivalent to eight gallons is something which is altogether too vague and indefinite to mean anything, such as parliament could intend that it means, or such as would be at all operative. To say that it shall be considered equivalent to a certain quantity is not certainly providing that it shall actually contain that quantity. It may be alleged to be a statutory declaration but as long as you have a can and that can shall be equivalent to eight gallons you can sell whatever you can get a person to take from you. At all exents, I think the Bill should be closely looked into from the professional, ministerial and legal standpoints.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS. (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say just a word in reference to this Bill. I think it is a very desirable thing that something of this kind should be passed. In reference to the remarks from my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), I just wish to say this : He says that he is afraid that a large number of cans which carry milk to creameries and cheese factories would become useless because they would not hold the exact amount of eight gallons. I would just like to say that cheese factories and creamaries do not buy milk. They take the milk from the farmers and make it up into cheese and butter for so much a pound. Here is another point in connection with the transportation of cream and milk on the railways. This matter came up at our board meeting on Friday last. We had quotations from the express company stating that they would take an eight gallon can a certain distance for so much. But in every case they wished it to be distinctly understood that these cans should hold eight gallons, no more, no less. If we had a law passed whereby one of these cans would be measured and stamped so that we would know that it held exactly eight gallons we would get over one of those difficulties that we have in connection with the express companies and railway companies in carrying our cream to the factories. There is another class of dealers who retail milk in cities and towns. They buy

their milk at so much a can. It is a question very frequently whether the can holds eight gallons or not. Sometimes it does and sometimes it does not. They would like to have the can stamped so that they would know when they buy a can of milk they buy a certain quantity. I think this Ilill is a good measure, and as to the statement that cans might become useless if it passed, I think there is no difficulty in that respect. I do not think there is anything in that at all.

Mr. Speaker, I have no objection to allow this Bill to stand until the lion. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) is present. I may say that we are not in this Bill establishing a new term. Some hon. members think that we are establishing a new term, the fact is that milk is sold now by the can. Three thousand cans a day come into the city of Toronto alone. What is a can of milk ? Can anybody tell ? Is there anything on the statute-book to tell how much a can contains-whether it is four, or six or ten gallons ? Nothing at all. This Bill may possibly have been a little more clearly worded, but the idea is a good one. It is to determine, when a man buys a can of milk, how much he has to get. The farmers are losing on every can of milk they sell in Toronto and Montreal from one-half, to two-thirds of a gallon. This may be a simple thing for some people but it is an important tiling for the farmers of York, Peel, Halton and all around the city of Toronto. I am surprised that the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) has raised objections to this Bill, when I consider the number of milk cans that come in from this county. The farmers of this county want this Bill to become law. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) I am sure, is in favour of this Bill because his constituents are largely interested in it and it will do no harm. The Bill simply determines what must be the quantity which a man must deliver when he sells a can of milk. If a can holds ten gallons, there is a can and one-fourth, if it holds nine gallons, a can and an eighth, if it holds seven gallons, seven-eighths of a can. There might only be four gallons, and if so, there is a gallon measure established by the department and you can easily determine whether there are four or five gallons in the can.
What is the object of providing another standard measure ? Why is it not just as well to say seven gallons to seven-eighths of a can ?
Seven gallons ?
The hon. gentleman says that if a can holds seven gallons it will be the equivalent of seven-eights of a can.
They are now using the can as a measure.
There is nothing to compel the farmer to sell by the can.
How are the farmers losing.

Because the dealers make the can, and they make it to contain eight and a half gallons and sometimes more, and the farmer loses half a gallon on each can. I do not wonder at the horn member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) being opposed to this Bill because the milk dealers in his constituency are up in arms against it. They are getting an extra half gallon on every can without paying for it. I am speakiug for the farmers who sell the milk, and I say they should not be obliged to furnish any more milk than they are paid for.

If I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) aright the farmers up in his section of the country do not know when they get a can whether it contains eight gallons or eight gallons and a half. They must be as simple as they were when they voted for the hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) under the supposition that lie was a protectionist. The man that is silly enough to order an eight gallon can and to take a can that contains eight gallons and a half deserves to be fooled. But what can be said of the hon. gentleman's electors when they were fooled into voting for him as a protectionist, and now he comes down here with his soul overburdened for the farmers interests and every time he gets a chance to vote for protection he votes against it.

I desire to make a personal explanation. The hon. gentleman from West York (Mr. Campbell) expresses surprise that I should! oppose this Bill. I wish to state that 1 emphatically declare that I do not want to oppose the Bill. He simply put that language into my mouth. I was not opposing the Bill by any means; I was simply endeavouring to get it into proper shape.

I am in favour of some change in the law as it now stands in respect to the sale of milk. In the county I have the honour to represent there is very general complaint that the farmers are not properly treated by those who purchase the milk in the large cities. I think, however, that the hon. member (Mr. Campbell) has not been careful enough in the preparation of his Bill. The Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) gave him a very heavy rebuke when he told the hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) that his Bill was open to very grave objection, and so I will reserve my remarka until the Bill comes before the House in proper shape. In the meantime I would suggest to the hon. member (Mi-. Campbell) that he should consult with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) and the Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. Mr. Bernier) so that he may draw up a proper Bill,

because I believe that this is a matter that should engage the serious attention of the government. There has been very great complaint for many years, especially in the neighbourhood of Toronto, and it is my opinion that parliament should take means to protect the honest farmer who is every day selling very large quantities of milk in -the centres of population.

I do not know enough of the particular circumstances of the case to express an opinion as to whether or not it is necessary to have a further standard of quantity. To judge from the speeches of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) he is seeking to establish a new standard of quantity for the sale of milk, but his Bill does not at all make provision for that. If he means what he says, then the language of his Bill falls very far short of its object. The objection taken by the Minister of Inland Revenue and the Minister of Railways and Canals is well founded in that respect. 1 thought the hon. gentleman was not going to permit milk to be sold except in eight gallon cans, but apparently lie does not intend that, although the Bill sounds as much like that as it does anything else. Assuming that the principle of the Bill is good, my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) will have to reconsider the wording of it very carefully, because in its present shape it would leave the law in a very much worse state than at present.
Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. T. THOMPSON (Haldimand and Monck).
speechtext: Mr. Speaker. During my absence from the House for a moment, a Bill standing in my name was called, and with the consent of the House I would like it to be taken up again. I refer to Bill (No. 24) entitled an Act to extend the Power of Loan Companies. It was threshed out iu the Committee on Banking and Commerce, and there was no objection taken to it. I wish to have the Bill considered in committee and read a third time.

With the consent of the House that may be done.
House went into Committee on the Bill.
On section 1,

That section seems to go pretty far. I suppose it has been fully considered by the Committee on Banking and Commerce ; but suppose, for example, that a loan company wishes to invest in the stock of a mining company, it might be a pretty speculative matter. The only pre-requisite imposed by this Bill is that the mining company should be one incorporated by the parliament of Canada. I may say that I am a member of the Committee on Banking and Commerce, but I
must acknowledge my fault in not being present when this Bill was considered.
Mr. THOMPSON (Haldimand and Monck),
I may explain to my hon. friend that this clause is exactly the same as what appears in the General Loan Companies Act of 1899, with the exception that the word ' future ' has been inserted to make it applicable to future provinces that come into the confederation, as well as to existing provinces. It is not extending the powers of loan companies at all, but is giving them the same powers that companies incorporated under the Act of 1899 enjoy, nothing more nor less.

If it is a bad provision, the fact that other companies have the right to do the same thing does not make it any better. That might be a good reason for amending the Act to which my hon. friend has referred by limiting the powers of these companies. I would like to know how it strikes my hon. friend the Finance Minister. These loan companies are regarded as pretty safe investments for the estates of people who desire to be very secure ; and yet this provision gives them a very wide scope for the investment of their funds, and possibly parliament may have gone a little further in the Act to which my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) refers than it should have gone.

The question has been very fully considered in times past, and I think the legislation adopted in the General Loan Companies' Act was regarded on the whole as safe. When the effect of this Bill is simply to bring the companies of earlier incorporation under the same standard as those incorporated later, I do not see how we can refuse it, Whether, speaking generally, we have made the powers of loan companies too broad, is a fair subject for consideration ; but I do not think we should be doing wrong by putting all the companies on the same footing.
Does this apply to companies operating under a provincial charter ?
No. I think the company referred to was operating under a Dominion charter.

We know there have been mining stocks in Canada which have dropped from 350 down to 12 iu the space of a few months. If one of these companies happens to have been incorporated under an Act of the parliament of Canada, this provision would permit a loan company to invest in it. I do not think that advisable, even if we have passed legislation to that effect. However, the government is responsible for this legislation, and I bring my objection now to the attention of the. hon. Minister of Finance, protesting, as far as I am concerned, that I do not think it

desirable to give a loan company tlie wide powers conferred on it by this section.

I may say that when the Act was before the committee a number of members opposed it strongly. Personally, I held the same view then that I hold to-day, that we were giving too wide powers to these companies. It was said that if we gave these wide powers to them other companies which had not equal powers would come and claim the right to have them ; and this is just what has happened. I agree with every word that has been said by my hon. friend beside me (Mr. Borden, Halifax), that we are giving powers that are altogether too wide.

I am rather glad to find that view prevailing, because I admit that the tendency of our legislation in this House is to be rather too liberal to the companies that come before us. I would rather see their powers somewhat restricted instead of being extended. Now that the matter has been brought to my attention, I will have it looked into ; but in the meantime, I think we should give the same powers to one company that we have given to others, and, if there is to be a change, let the change apply to all.
Bill reported.

DEMERS (St. Johns and Iberville) (Translation) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 22) to amend the Supreme Court and Exchequer Court Acts.
Mr. Speaker, I feel it is incumbent on me to reassure this House. The judiciary is part and parcel of our body politic. To seek its overthrow, would be to shake the very foundation on which the state rests. On the contrary, to work towards its betterment and improvement is, to my mind, the part of good citizenship.
The uninitiated who witness the glorious uncertainty of the law, the endless conflicts going on among the courts and often among the judges of the same court, may be tempted to take the view that the best judgment is the quickest and that courts of appeal should be dispensed with. That is a serious mistake. Courts are apt to err in rendering hasty judgments, and that in itself is sufficient reason for having courts of appeal. Hence, to the question : What are the courts whose judgments should be final, Bentham unhesitatingly answers : None. But, if courts of appeal are a necessity, it does not follow that they may not become too numerous.
In a country like ours, where all members of the bar take up the same studies, where the skill and experience required by the judges in the various courts are similar, it cannot be argued with seriousness that the judges of courts of appeal, whatever be their jurisdiction, are necessarily superior Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
in knowledge to the judges of the superior courts.
If the former are called upon to revise the judgments rendered by the latter, it is solely for the purpose of avoiding mistakes due to hasty decisions. That is all, so far as clear cases are concerned. As regards doubtful ones, they cannot be ended too soon in the interest of the parties. That is a safe rule, to my mind, when private interests only are at stake. The question is a different one if you are dealing with the political and commercial interests of the country. The uniformity of the laws in this connection could not be imperilled without causing an injury to the people as a whole.
My conclusion, then, is that in the case of laws concerning the whole empire, the final decisions, from the nature of things, should rest with the highest tribunal of the empire : in the case of laws interesting Canada only, the decision of our Supreme Court should be final ; and when the citizens of one province only are concerned, the courts in that province should be left to deal with the case. In questions of law, as in matters of ethics, interest is the measure of actions. In cases where the Privy Council has been called upon to give its interpretation of the British North America Act, 1807, or of some of the Imperial Acts, its jurisdiction was always looked to with respect and favour by all classes. The provinces will not forget that the Privy Council has at all times shown itself the custodian of their rights, and it would be a great mistake on their part to endeavour to escape its jurisdiction.
But to call upon that tribunal to settle a petty dispute over a party wall, is dragging it out of its proper realm and lowering its prestige. The needy litigant who is forced "to appear before these far-away courts, rightly wonders at it, and the public mind is disturbed, as it was in the ease of (lie Canadian Pacific Railway Company vs. Roy. This morning's papers reproduce an article from a paper in London, going to say that the organization of the Privy Council as regards colonial matters is faulty and should be modified. That view is not a new one. Here is what Lord Brougham said as early as 1828, regarding the Privy Council :
It is obvious that from the mere distance of those colonies and the immense variety of matters arising in them, foreign to our habits, and beyond the scope of our knowledge, any judicial tribunal in this country must, of necessity, be an extremely inadequate court of review.
These remarks are applicable equally well to the Supreme Court. If after twenty-seven years' experience, I make bold to propose that the constitution of that court be amended, it goes without saying, Mr. Speaker, that it is for me to prove that it has not come up to the expectations of its promoters. I shall do so with all the respect due to the powers that be, but at the same time with the freedom inspired by a strong belief.

Fur from me the thought of dragging into tills debate the distinguished members of the judiciary. Some papers have iu this respect committed excesses which the public conscience condemns.
My indictment will be short. I charge the Supreme Court of Canada with having failed to secure the confidence of the country.
Last year, ' La Patrie,' one of the important papers supporting the government at tiietime, stated: 'The Supreme Court, from the start, was unpopular in all the provinces.' For the last ten years, at almost every session of parliament, its abolition was sought, and one of the present judges, taking the moderate view which X now take, moved in 1881, to have its constitution amended.
The Supreme Court, as we know, was established in 1875. Although it was a government measure, several supporters of the party in power, considered themselves bound in duty to vote against the Act, particularly Mr. Becbard and Mr. Bourassa, both representatives of the counties which I now represent. In 1881, Mr. Girouard, who is today one of the judges of that court, introduced a Bill to restrict the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.
That same year, Mr. Landry, now a member of the Senate, introduced a Bill for the abolition of the Supreme Court. And in 1881, Sir John Macdonald said:
Are we to appoint a certain number of judges ad hoc, taken from the judiciary or the bar of Canada, to complete the personnel of that tribunal, when cases from the province of Quebec have to be adjudicated on, or are we to adopt some other means ? I would not like to say, and if the Supreme Court is to be upheld, we shall have to find a solution that will do away with the dissatisfaction that prevails, at all events, among the French Canadians of Lower Canada.
In 1882, Sir Alexander Campbell introduced in the Senate a Bill to amend the constitution of the Supreme Court. Not only did the French speaking population find fault with that court, but the English speaking people as well were dissatisfied with it. Let me quote from the ' Legal News,' the organ of the English speaking lawyers. At page 140 of Yol. I., we read :
1	L. N., p. 140. The Supreme Court at present is looked upon with great distrust.
2	L. N., p. 161. This is saying nothing new to lawyers in this province, for it has long been evident that some of them, as well as their clients, are unwilling to take any case to Ottawa which can possibly be carried to England. The reason for this state of things is to he found in the dissimilarity of the law in the different provinces from which the judges have been taken, and the fact that the cases from this province are generally supposed to be left chiefly to the two members who were appointed from the bench and bar of Quebec.
4. L.N., p. 74. The dissatisfaction of Ontario and Quebec has manifested itself with considerable violence and some reason.
The province of Quebec was not the only one to complain. The province of Ontario
took the same position from the beginning, and up to this day, complaints have not varied. I may be permitted to quote the following extracts from the Canada Law Journal, the great law periodical of Ontario. Canada Law Journal, 1879 :
The profession, as a whole, have not that confidence in it which should appertain to a court of final resort ; for example, there is hardly a lawyer, in this province at least, who would not, on a question of Ontario law, prefer the opinion of our Court of Appeal, or even of one of our Superior Courts. ... It is also manifest, that the court, so far, has been a disappointment.
Canada Law Journal, 1880 :
There are some who think the best way to improve the Supreme Court would be to improve it off of the face of the earth. We trust some less heroic remedy may be found, though the court certainly has, both collectively and through some of its members, on several occasions and in various unnecessary ways, endeavoured to commit suicide.
Canada Law Journal, 1882:
The court has so far been a failure, partly owing to the inherent difficulties of our confederation, partly to the fact that the best talent has not always for some reason or other been taken advantage of, and partly owing to the difficulties and infirmities of a personal nature which we do not care to enlarge upon.
Canada Law Journal, 1892 :
The court has not in the past commanded the confidence of the public to the extent that the court of final resort for the Dominion should.
Canada Law Journal, 1895 :
May we be forgiven for venturing to suggest that the opinion of the profession is that, though the Supreme Court contains much valuable judicial material, it is not the strongest, does not command the greatest confidence.
Canada Law Journal, 1896, p. C4G :
This court has long lacked the confidence of the bar, both in the English-speaking provinces and in Quebec.
Canada I,aw Journal, 1902, p. 63 :
Speaking generally, parties do not go to the Supreme Court because they expect more careful consideration or better exposition of the law, but rather on the off chance of a reversal by another set of judges, gambling on the uncertainty of the law. Let it be remembered, however, that in the Supreme Court there are never more than two judges from any one province. To these two, or perhaps to one of them, is often in effect left the criticism of three, four or five judgments of men of at least equal attainments, and having special knowledge of the law affecting their various provinces. Is it likely that a reversal under such conditions would be considered a satisfactory adjudication ?
From tlie same periodical, same year, p. 178 :
We have not said and do not mean that the Supreme Court has not occasionally laid down the law more correctly than the courts referred to, hut we repeat w'hat we have already said.

that, speaking generally, the appellate courts in the various provinces stand higher in the estimation of their bars than does the Supreme Court of Canada. For example, what professional man can be found in Ontario who would prefer the opinion of the men composing the Supreme Court Bench to those now sitting in the Court of Appeal at Osgoode Hall.
Lord Dufferin, at the time our Supreme Court was established, referring to the Supreme Court of the United States, said :
Witness the respect and deference with which the chief court of the United States is quoted by British and European jurists.
The Supreme Court of Canada, on the contrary, continues to be looked upon, ns stated by the Legal News, 1 with great distrust.' Are we going to perpetuate this state of things ? Yes, if we persist in closing our eyes to the cause of the evil. This is to be found either in the inherent constitution of the body or in its constituent parts. I am aware that the judges of that court have often been attacked. But to my mind, Mr. Speaker, nothing is more unfair. The proof is this : The judges of that court have been chosen from among men who had previously distinguished themselves. To refer only to the province of Quebec, did any one ever doubt of the attainments of the Hon. Mr. Fournier, Minister of Justice, or of the Hon. Mr. Justice Taschereau, who is one of a family of jurists and who has written highly esteemed works, or of the Hon. Mr. Justice Gir-ouard, who had an extensive practice in commercial matters, and has made a reputation for himself through his legal writings ? Besides, to my mind, a peremptory argument is the following : the original members have been replaced and the body is still diseased. The ailment is therefore a constitutional one. The jurisdiction of the court in provincial matters is unwarranted. The right of the Supreme Court to deal with provincial matters is doubtful, if we consider only the wording of the law ; it is more so, if we take into account the spirit of the constitution. But there cannot be any doubt left if we look at it from the point of view of common sense : this does away with it entirely.
Section 101 of our Constitution reads as follows :
The parliament of Canada may, notwithstanding anything in this Act, from time to time, provide for the constitution, maintenance and organization of a general court of appeal, and for the establishment of any additional courts for the better administration of the laws of Canada.
Do the words ' for the better administration of the laws of Canada ' apply to the whole sentence; that is the vexed point. Mr. Speaker. The section itself would lead us to doubt it.
True, the Supreme Court has decided this point in its favour in a case of the Saint Jean Baptiste Association vs. Brault, in which my colleague the hon. member for Ottawa appeared. But a judge should not Mr. DEMERS (St. Johns and Iberville).
be expected to decide against himself in his own case. The court by that judgment maintained its jurisdiction in matters of civil law' ; but what it was not in its power to do-what it is in the power of no tribunal to do-was to dispel the doubt existing in the minds of the people. We are familiar with that ancient custom whereby sovereigns attempted to establish their right to the throne by having the lords of the land to take the oath of allegiance. But that would not prevent the people from being in doubt. Opinion persists in spite of edicts.
Now% if it wras in order for two of the present judges, when members of this House, one in 1875, the other in 1881, to state their belief that this court was exercising usurped powers, I should be permitted in 1902 to entertain some doubt on the matter.
But when I take into account the spirit of our constitution, w'hich has for its mainstay provincial autonomy, my doubts are greatly strengthened ; and they materialize in the form of the following agreement, which, I think, will have some weight.
The legislative and the judiciary powers are correlated. There is no judiciary power that does not rest on legislative authority ; and no legislative authority that is not sanctioned by the judiciary power. Then, section 92 of the British North American Act enacts that in certain matters the legislative power will be vested exclusively in the provinces. Does that not signify that the judiciary power will be, as well.
But in one respect there cannot be any doubt ; it is this : the constitution of that court is repugnant to reason.
Oni that point I could not do better than to quote the opinion expressed by Mr. McCuaig, in the Hansard of 1881 : Mr. Mc-Cuaig said :
The opinion entertained by the majority of the inhabitants of the county I represent is this : We have a Supreme Court composed of six men, two from Ontario, two from Quebec, and two from the maritime provinces. As I understand the matter, the two judges from Ontario are not at all familiar with the laws of Quebec, while the two judges from the maritime provinces are not familiar with the laws of either Ontario or Quebec. Now, in Ontario we have an Appeal Court, composed of four judges of high legal attainments and well qualified to decide finally upon most every case that comes before them. But a case taken from our Court of Appeal, presided over by four of the best judges of Ontario, may be taken to the Supreme Court, and their judgment overruled by the four judges from Quebec and the maritime provinces, not at all familiar with our laws. That is not at all calculated to create any confidence in the decisions of the Supreme Court.
Last year, tbe House had the advantage of listening to an able speech from the hon. member for Hants in favour of uniformity in our laws. It is not my intention to refer to the debate which follow'ed. The inference which I desire to draw from it, is that laws differ greatly from one province to the

other. In case it was desired to bring about uniformity, would not advice be sought from jurists in each of the provinces ? Why V Because life is all- .rt. and the way that leads to knowledge is a long and winding one. To acquire a thorough knowledge of the laws in each of the provinces is a difficult task ; but that does not suffice. I am of opinion, said a latin writer that theory without prac-, tice will not give a perfect knowledge of law. The laws of the various provinces, in accordance with this principle, prevent any who have not practiced, their profession during a certain number of years, from exercising judiciary functions. Nevertheless, we have here judges who decide in last resort on laws which they have neither studied nor practiced.
And there arc those who wonder that such a court should be unpopular ! Some periodicals, some papers ask that the best men be appointed. They are losing their eyes to the light. The evil is apparent : if the judge is to apply the law, he should be familiar with the law.
It may be stated : If he docs not know the law when appointed, he will make himself familiar with it. Here is d'Aguesseau's answer to this :
Amid a variety of positive enactments, based on the customs of peoples, or on the sovereign will of the legislator, this body of laws has nevertheless its rules and principles. To become conversant with them, shall we wait for the crafty and interested party to lay before us fragmentary excerpts, skilfully selected and artfully arranged ; and shall the judge, whose part It is to instruct men in the law, be content with learning it in the pleadings of litigants ?
Lord Brougham, in ills great speech on judicial reform, on February 7, 1828, referring to judges in India, said :
In total ignorance of the manners, the customs, the prejudices, possibly of the language of those upon whose affairs and conduct he is to sit in judgment, and by whose testimony he is to peruse his inquiries, and very possibly equally uninformed of the laws he is to administer-he must be wholly dependent upon his pundit for direction, both as to matter of fact and matter of law.
Mr. Speaker, how are we to expect that, even in time, our brightest lawyers in the provinces, our magistrates, and all who have spent days and nights pouring over the study of provincial laws, and who, nevertheless, have to acknowledge their ignorance, will lay their case without reserve or reticence before a tribunal constituted as is the Supreme Court ? That was possible in times gone by when authority was supreme ; it cannot be expected to-day, when right is everything.
It is that lack of confidence which has been the incentive of the numerous attacks to which the Supreme Court has been subjected. Therefore, its constitution is defective.
The Bill submitted to your consideration
has for its purpose to make the Supreme
Court a Federal Court. The court will thus gain in prestige what it loses in scope. The clause suggested is taken from the constitution of the United States.
I quoted, a few moments ago, the opinion of Lord Dufferii regarding the Supreme Court of the United States. I.et me quote also from Alexis de Toequeville :	The Supreme Court, he said, is on a higher plane than any known tribunal, both as regards its powers and the kind of people over whom it exercises those powers.
Professor Dicey, referring to the Supreme Court of the United States writes :
Nothing in the institutions of America has exacted more admiration among foreigners than the position given under the constitution to the federal judiciary.
In consequence, several confederacies have followed suit; it will suffice to mention Mexico, Columbia and Switzerland. Were we to give our Supreme Court a truly federal character, what respect would it not command ? Courts of law being tribunals of compulsory arbitration, they should, like Caesar's wife, be above suspicion. Our Supreme Court at present resembles the sphinx, a monster, neither man nor beast, and which the passer-by seeks to avoid. I would have it resemble the shining statue of Memnon, which emitted harmonious sounds at sunrise, and to which would come all those seeking justice and truth.
Mr. Speaker, I move the second reading of this Bill.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, as the hon. leader of the opposition understands French and was able to follow the speech made by the hon. member for St. Johns and Iberville (Mr. Demers), I shall give in French the few remarks I have to offer.
The hon. member for St. John and Iberville, who just moved the second reading of the Bill, made a very broad charge against the Supreme Court : that of not having secured the confidence of the people either in Ontario or in Quebec. What proofs did he bring forward in support of his charge ? A statement in ' La Patrie ' to the effect that the Supreme Court did not command public confidence. Also quotations to the same effect from the ' Canada Law Journal,' since 1882.
That is a very hard charge to make against the highest tribunal in the Dominion ; and the only evidence in support of it are extracts from ' La Patrie ' and the ' Canada Law Journal,' a periodical edited by some one who likely has some old grudge against the court.
When the hon. member, after bringing forth that general charge, entered into particulars, some statements he made struck me. He likened the Supreme Court to a monster; hut at the same time, spoke highly of the judges who compose that tribunal.

They were, he said, honest, fair-minded men, eminent jurists, whose knowledge of the law was all that could be desired. I should have preferred if he had dealt with the living and left the dead alone. However, he thought fit to follow the opposite course. I regret that notice was not given me until this evening that this Bill was to come up for discussion. I would have been better prepared to reply to the eloquent and learned disquisition from my hon. friend, the member for St. Johns and Iberville.
His main contention is that the Supreme Court, as now organized, is unconstitutional. That is- to say, when the said court was established in 1876, that establishment was not constitutional. And in support of this statement my hon. friend quoted the opinions expressed by Judges Tasehereau and Mills, the latter to-day a judge of the Supreme Court. I have read Mr. Mills' speech, and I believe he does express doubts as to the constitutionality of that tribunal. So does Mr. Tasehereau, and so does Mr. Moss, now a judge at Toronto. Mr. Tascho-reau was at one time member for Montmagny in this House, and he is to-day a judge of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec.
But from what was said when the question came up for discussion, at the time of confederation, it is easy to find out what was the intention of those who inserted in the British North America Act a clause providing for the establishment of a Supreme Court. Sir John Macdonald spoke as follows :-
There are many arguments for and against the establishment of such a court, but it was thought wise and expedient to put into the constitution a power of the general legislature, that, if after full consideration they think it advisable to establish a general Court of Appeal from all the Superior Courts of all the provinces, they may do so.
The following is the opinion expressed by Sir George Etienne Cartier :
Accordingly, when we have lived some years under the federal regime, the urgent need of such a Court of Appeal with jurisdiction in such matters will be felt, and, if it is created, I it will be fit that its jurisdiction should extend I to civil causes which might arise in the several confederate provinces, because it will necessarily be composed of the most eminent judges in the different provinces, of the jurists whose reputation stands highest, of men, in short, profoundly skilled in the jurisprudence of each of the provinces which they will respectively represent. Well, if this court is called upon, for instance, to give final judgment on a judgment rendered by a Lower Canada court, there will be among the judges on the bench, men perfectly versed in the knowledge of the laws of that section of the confederation, will be able to. give the benefits of their lights to the other judges sitting with them.
The honourable Mr. Justice Fournier, who introduced the Bill constituting the Supreme Court, stated that this tribunal, as organized, was strictly constitutional. But let Hon. Mr. CARROLL.
us forego that question, and deal with the actual facts. The Supreme Court has been in existence twenty-seven years. At the outset, many complaints were made against it. I remember reading, in the report of the discussion which took place when Mr. Girou-ard introduced a Bill to the same purpose as the present one, in the House. But who were the complainants ? Members, unsuccessful litigants, who had had cases before that court and had not succeeded in having their claims sustained. That was the cause of much discontent for six or eight years. But since 1882, has there been any serious cause of complaint proven against the Supreme Court ?
The hon. member for St. Johns and Iberville, who earefully worked up his case, could only find, after going through the volumes of ' Hansard ' since 1882, such extracts as he quoted from the Canada Law Journal, in support of his contention. I admit there is something abnormal about the constitution of the Supreme Court In the fact that there are only two judges familiar with the French laws of the province of Quebec. But I contend that this defect is not of such great consequence as some would have us believe. The French law is based on the Roman law, and so is tlie English law. It may be that, as regards questions of procedure, the inconvenience is felt to a greater degree, but it is a poor compliment to pay to our civil laws to represent them as a' mystery which no one can solve. If that argument had any weight it would apply more particularly to the Privy Council whose members are not supposed to know any thing at all about the civil law of the province of Quebec, while there are two judges of the Supreme jOourt specially conversant with that law.
I am in favour of maintaining the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, as I believe the provinces are not yet ripe for judicial autonomy. To convince oneself of the truth of what I say, it will suffice to observe what is going on. Notwithstanding all the respect I have for the courts of appeal of my province, notwithstanding the attainments, integrity and impartiality of the judges composing them, I say that the Supreme Court, as well as the Privy Council, serve, so to speak, as safety valves, and that it is a good thing for litigants to have a court of last resort outside of the provincial domain.
See what is going on in Ontario. There, judges of the High Court have been made the object of attacks in the legislature to a degree unknown in my province.
But there is another reason, of a more practical character for upholding the Supreme Court. Should that Bill become law, the maritime provinces, which have no courts of appeal, would be without an appellate tribunal to resort to. The answer given to this argument is that such courts of appeal should be provided for those pro-

vinces. Well, let these courts of appeal for the maritime provinces be constituted first, and then parliament may be called upon to vote the Bill proposed by the hon. member. For reasons of a practical character, the government cannot allow the Bill to become law just now. It may be voted a few years hence when our judicial system has been reorganized.
speakername: The SOLICITOR GENERAL (Hon. H. G. Carroll, Kamouraska).

speechtext:
(Translation.) I did not inted to address the House after the hon. Solicitor General. But as the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) has not thought fit to be present here tonight, to defend the policy of the government, relieving himself of the burden on the hon. the Solicitor General, I deem it my duty as a French member from the province of Quebec, to give my support to the hon. member for St. Johns and Iberville, in respect to the Bill, the second reading of which was moved this evening.
The province of Quebec, more especially, suffers from the judgments of the Supreme Court. And it is made to suffer the more because the majority of the judges of that court, consisting of talented men, no doubt, are utterly ignorant of French laws and customs. The province of Quebec wishes to remain French, and to attain that object, it must keep its civil laws and have judges who studied and understand its laws.
The hon. Solicitor General, in support of a cause which he unwillingly upholds, argued that the maritime provinces had no court of appeal. That is so, but it is an easy matter to establish such courts. There can be no difficulty in giving those provinces what they are in need of, and it is unfair that the province of Quebec should be made to suffer any longer for such trifling reasons.
We are all aware that, at the time the Supreme Court was constituted, the members from the province of Quebec almost unanimously opposed the Bill for the reasons given to-night by the member for St. Johns and Iberville. The majority of the judges of the Supreme Court are not at all conversant with the French civil laws ; and the barristers in the province of Quebec, knowing as they do that these judges are not competent to deal with matters of French civil law, generally advise their clients to limit their claims to $1,999, in order to preclude any possibility of appeal to the Supreme Court. The hon. the Solicitor General stated that it was in the interest of the province generally, and of the province of Quebec in particular, to uphold the Supreme Court, which played the part of a safety valve, its judges being outside of provincial influences. I feel I am in duty bound to say that, as regards the province of Quebec, the courts of appeal now in existence answer all purposes of that kind. All thejudges who sit in those courts are really qualified, and soar above the disputes of litigants.
As I stated a moment ago, I was not aware that the Bill was to be discussed this
evening. I regret it, for had I known, I would have made it a point to get ready for the debate. It would have been an easy matter to find arguments in support of the Bill. However, I have no hesitation in saying that the case made by my hon. friend in support of his Bill was carefully prepared and clearly laid out. The House should pass this Bill at once, even if it were only through consideration for the province of Quebec. The supporters of the government are largely from that province, and a good way for the government to show their thankfulness to Quebec would be to comply with the wishes of the members from that province, and to do away with the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in matters of civil law, which would then be referred in last resort to the highest court of appellate jurisdiction in the province.

I merely want to add a few words to what has been said, and I think it is proper and a simple matter of courtesy to our Englishspeaking colleagues that a few words should be said in English on this subject; not that much practical result will come from this debate at present, but I believe that this parliament and government will be forced before long to remove the sentiment of distrust that is growing in the province of Quebec against the Supreme Court. It may be said that the word ' distrust ' is a strong one, but it is that which was used by my hon. friend and which he has taken from another authority. As my hon. friend from St. Johns and Iberville (Mr. Demers) has said, that sentiment does not arise, and has never arisen, from any personal animosity against the members who compose the Supreme Court of Canada. But, as my hon. friend has said-and this is the one line of argument on which I desire to insist-there is something in the Supreme Court that shocks common sense. Apart from the legal aspect of the question, upon which of course I would not dare to express my views, the federal Act creating this federal court authorized it to act as the highest court of appeal in all matters and laws affecting the Dominion, whether provincial or federal. The parliament of Canada has thought proper to give to that court an appellate jurisdiction in all cases in which a higher amount than a certain prescribed sum is at stake, affecting the civil and other laws that are within the exclusive legislative powers of the provinces; so that certain laws and matters, in respect of which we have no power whatever to legislate, in respect of which the supreme power of legislation lies in the provinces and in respect of which provincial tribunals have been established to adjudicate, the parliament of Canada has brought within the jurisdiction of this federal court which it has established. Therefore, we have given to a court created by this parliament jurisdiction to decide on matters concerning which we have no power

whatever to legislate. That being the case, there is at the basis ot the creation of the Supreme Court of Canada something, it seems to me, that shocks common sense. My hon. friend the Solicitor General lias said that in the beginning there were some complaints against the Supreme Court, but that those arose from political causes and came from members of parliament who considered themselves aggrieved by decisions of the Supreme Court in electiou matters. I shall not refer at all to that part of the question, but I say that although complaints may not often have been made in the parliament of Canada, nevertheless they still exist. As my hon. friend from St. Johns and Iberville (Mr. Demers) says, we have sometimes had complaints made on account of the personnel of the judges composing some of the courts of the provinces. At times it has been urged that the Court of Appeals of the province of Quebec does not now enjoy the esteem in which it was held some years ago on account of its personnel, but we have never heard any complaints with regard to its jurisdiction. It has never been urged that its jurisdiction should be amended. It lias been said that the government did not always choose the best men to sit in that court. But as regards the Supreme Court of Canada, complaints have been made that cases which were decided by one of the judges of the Superior Court and three judges of the Court of Review and five judges of the Court of Appeals of that province, or in all, nine judges conversant with the laws of the province of Quebec, were afterwards decided by a tribunal on which there were only two judges who could be considered as authorities on the laws of that province. So that you have, as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, placed in the hands of two men the right to revise the judgments of nine other men equally versed in our laws. My hon. friend has said that the right of appeal to the Supreme Court and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is a safeguard to the litigants of our province, who might not be satisfied with the decisions of the final court of appeals of that province. Well, the same thing might be said of any tribunal. Litigants that are not satisfied with the judgment of the Privy Council would say that there should be another safeguard. But now we have an Australasian colony, one where there is no race question to deal with, and which is known as being the most loyal of the British colonies-I refer to New Zealand-complaining bitterly as to the way the British Privy Council has dealt with some of the judicial matters of that colony. Therefore, the fact that complaints may arise against one tribunal is no reason for saying that we should give more appeals. In France, I believe, appeals are limited to two courts, whatever may be the amount involved. One is the court of appeal-I do not know the name it bears-and then the court Mr. BOURASSA.
of cassation. Beyond this, there is no appeal. In England there are less appeals, I believe, than with us. In this country where we are more distant, where the interests are smaller and the litigants are poorer- where everything is against the multiplicity of appeals-we have more appeals than they have in England, or in the republic of France, or in the United States. My hon. friend from St. Johns and Iberville has quoted words from Lord Dufferin which apply most perfectly to this case, words spoken by him when the Supreme Court was created. He expressed the hope that the Supreme Court of Canada would attain an equally high position in popular respect with that of the Supreme Court of the United States. As a rule, comparisons between the constitution of Canada and the constitution of the United States are entirely in favour of Canada. But this is one particular point in which we might take a lesson from our neighbours. As is well known to the members of this House, whether they belong to the legal profession or not, the magistrates of the United States do not enjoy, on the average, the same respect that our judges or the judges of England enjoy. How is it, then, that the Supreme Court of the United States is the one tribunal in that country that has never been attacked by any class of men, but, at times, has saved the dignity and future of the republic ? This arises from the fact that the legislators in the United States have vested in the Supreme Court only such powers as might be exercised properly by such a tribunal, and have prevented small cases that might cause useless friction between the litigants and the highest tribunal of the republic being brought before that court. The jurisdiction is limited to the same power as those to which my hon. friend would like the Supreme Court of Canada to be limited. And what has been the result ? People know that when they appeal to the Supreme Court of the United States they appeal to a tribunal that has nothing to do with trifling matters, with small matters between individuals, but with matters designed to promote harmony between the citizens of the United States or between the states themselves, or to interpret the general laws of the republic or laws that might arouse conflict between the states. Here, it is entirely different. Not satisfied with the multiplied appeals that we have in the provinces, we have created a supreme body. Whatever be the legal power of the parliament of Canada at the time they created that Supreme Court, it is certainly against the spirit, if not the letter of the constitution, that the federal authorities should have the power to create another tribunal than one that would give uniform jurisprudence In matters of federal legislation. But I am quite positive, and common sense would tell us that the authors of confederation never contemplated-or, at least, it was not their main purpose-to create an appeal

body for the different provinces. What they meant, and what we should carry out-for, after all, the work of the fathers of the confederation is a work that may be changed once in a while, though, as a rule I am not in favour of changing the work of the authors of the constitution-is when we find in some of the subsequent legislation matters against the spirit of the constitution, we should come nearer to the spirit of the constitution, though we may break with the letter.	Can it have
been the intention of the fathers of the constitution to create a tribunal of appeal for the provinces ? It must have been their intention to create a supreme body that would enjoy the respect of the whole people of Canada and of the different governments of Canada ; therefore, a body that would be composed of men entirely versed in the law they were to interpret. But, as my hon. friend from St. Johns has said, when we have cases brought from the court of appeal of Quebec to the Supreme Court, we know-I have been a witness of it myself-that the lawyers from the province of Quebec find it necessary to make for some of the judges an elementary course in the law of our province, such as is given to the second year student. This is not a fact that is likely to raise our respect for the Supreme Court; and, our respect for the Supreme Court being diminished in ordinary legal matters when it is called upon to give interpretation on the main body of our provincial laws, in the reaction, we have less respect and consideration for I hem in matters in which they have perfect jurisdiction and in which they ought to be the supreme body. Therefore, for the safety of our constitution, for the harmony of the provinces, and in the interest of uniformity in our law and the giving to the provincial law the proper interpretation, they should deal with federal law, and should not have the power to pass judgment under the law of the different provinces. As my hon. friend lias said, in every province it is forbidden for a lawyer, although he may have practiced for twenty-five years in another province, to plead even an ordinary case before any of the courts of such province in which he is not a member of the bar, because he is supposed not to know the law of that province. But now, simply by an Act of this parliament, a man who would not be allowed to plead before a justice of the province of Ontario will come and give judgment as a final appeal against all judgments that may have been rendered by the high court of justice or the court of appeal of Ontario. And, in the same way, a lawyer who, because of his lack of legal knowledge, could not plead before the Superior Court of the province of Quebec, will, the day after lie is appointed to the Supreme Court, pass final judgments on matters that he does not know and will reverse the judgments of the Superior Court, the Court of Review and the Court of Appeal
of that province, courts that are composed of men who must have practiced .law in their province for at least ten years. I appeal to any man of common sense, whatever might be the letter of the constitution, whatever might be the intention of the men who created the Supreme Court, if the time lias not come to deal with this problem and put the Supreme Court in a position, not of less power and prestige, but of greater power and prestige, because their jurisdiction would be confined to matters that these judges will know?

The government can hardly realize the importance of this measure, otherwise we should not see the front benches opposite in their present condition. This is a Bill that proposes to take away about nine-tenths of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of Canada. We have not the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice or any other member of the cabinet in the House to consider it, except my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding).
I think therefore there must be some misapprehension in the minds of the members of the government as to what this Bill really means, or we would see some little attention paid to it by members of the government. Does the Minister of Finance realize what this Bill means ? Does he realize that it is one of the most important Bills touching the judiciary of this country that has ever been offered to this House ?	1 should think
that some members of the government, at least, would tell us what they are prepared to do with it, and that we would not see the spectacle in this parliament of its passing, as it actually did, the second reading a moment ago, and having this principle affirmed without a single member of the government except the Solicitor General, who addressed the House to some extent upon it, saying a single word about it. I do not think that seems to indicate that the Bill has received very much consideration at the hands of the government, or we would surely have heard something more about it.
Now I do not deny that there is something in the argument of my hon. friend from St. Johns and Iberville (Mr. Demers). I understand that gentlemen from the province of Quebec do not like very well to see the judgments of their own final courts overruled by the Supreme Court of Canada, and possibly, in some cases, when a judge from their own province may have sustained the judgments of the court below. I believe that has happened sometimes. Well, that happens sometimes in cases from other provinces. I myself, from the province of Nova Scotia, have known a unanimous judgment of the Supreme Court of my province overruled in the Supreme Court by a divided court, the majority of which included two judges from the province of Quebec. Of course these are circumstances that will

sometimes occur. But it does not necessarily tollow that you cannot have a Supreme Court of Canada that will do fairly good work.
