I acknowledge at once that, from the very constitution of that court, there may be to a certain extent a sort of inherent weakness in it; but I do not think It is a weakness that is not! capable of being overcome by appointing to that court the most eminent men that you can get in the whole of Canada, and appointing those men at a time of life when they can devote some time to the study of the laws of the different provinces. My horn friend emphasizes altogether too much the differences between the laws of the various provinces. Now take cases from the province of Quebec. You will find among them questions arising upon matters as to which the laws of all the provinces are practically the same. The laws of Quebec as well as of the other provinces are supposed to be founded on common sense. For example, take the provisions of the Code, they are in many respects very much like the provisions of our English common law. Our English Equity system is founded upon provisions of the civil law which is really very much the same as the system of law administerd in the province of Quebec to-day. Take all the statute law of Canada, take for example the Bills of Exchange Act, and you have the same provisions prevailing in all the provinces.
My hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bour-assa) spoke of counsel from one province not being fit to conduct a case before a magistrate in another province. My hon. friend is entirely mistaken. In the province of Nova Scotia we would be glad to welcome at our bar any member of the bar of the; province of Quebec, and admit him by courtesy to practise before our courts in any case in which he happened to be interested. That is done every day. Members of the bar of thej United States of America come into our courts in cases in which they have clients in the United States, and by courtesy are allowed to practise before our courts. Members of the bar of Ontario have, during the past year, appeared before our courts.
This privilege is reciprocal in the United States.

I know it is. I am only pointing out to the member for Labelle what perhaps he has not fully appreciated, that even as between ourselves and the various courts in the United States, the laws are so much the same that a man eminent in his profession in one place can practise with advantage in another place, and is allowed to do so as a matter of courtesy. So far as the laws of the maritime provinces and the laws of Ontario and the west are concerned, they are very much the same. There Is really no reason why a judge from the province of Ontario, or a judge from the maritime provinces, cannot deal successfully with cases coming from Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
a province in which he has not practised ; that is to say, a judge coming from the province of Ontario is fully capable of sitting in appeal on cases coming from the province of Nova Scotia, and I think judges and lawyers from the maritime provinces, assuming they are eminent men at the bar, are capable of dealing with cases that come from the province of Ontario, or Manitoba, or British Columbia.
Now it is not impossible, Mr. Speaker, to have a court that) will give satisfaction, although that court has to administer laws with which all the members of the court are not familiar. Take for instance, the Privy Council, referred to by the member for St. Johns and Iberville. The Privy Council, I think, has commanded the respect, not only of litigants but of lawyers from all parts of the British empire. The Privy Council administers, I suppose, twenty different systems of law, at least-I am speaking offhand-and administers laws with regard perhaps to thirty, forty or fifty different races. The Privy Council commands the respect, I believe, of my hon. friends of the bar of the province of Quebec-T have not heard anything to the contrary in the speech of the hon. member for St. Johns and Iberville. Well, the members of the Privy Council are not men who have made a special study of the laws of the province of Quebec, but I think on the whole, cases from that province that have gone to the Privy Council, as a general rule, have received the consideration which has entitled that judicial body to the respect of members of the bar from that province. The Supreme Court of the United States administers different systems of law. Is it not a fact that the state of Louisiana enjoys the advantage of a civil law which, to some extent, resembles that which prevails in the province of Quebec ?

New York has a code.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax. But I am speaking of an entirely different system of law. The state of Louisiana has a different system of law from most of the states comprising the American republic.
Has the Supreme Court of the United States jurisdiction over the state laws of Louisiana when they do not affect outsiders ?

I do not pretend to be very familiar with the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of the United States, but I should suppose that when a question of state law arose between the residents of that state and those of another state, the Supreme Court of the United States would have to deal with it.
That is what this Bill proposes to do.

Would not the Supreme Court of Canada, or the Supreme Court of the United States, be able to deal
MAY i, 1903
with the local laws in cases of that kind ? What makes the Supreme Court of Canada, or that of the United States, better able to deal with the laws of the provinces or of the states In such cases ?
It is a matter of necessity.

Why is there any necessity ? Why not, in that case, leave it to the law of the particular province in which the litigant resides, and from which the case comes on appeal, if you take it for granted that the ultimate tribunal is not capable of dealing satisfactorily with the question presented to its consideration ? That argument carried to its logical conclusion would exclude ai Supreme Court of Canada altogether. The argument of my hon. friend from St. Johns and Iberville, if carried to its logical conclusion, would abolish the Supreme Court of Canada, and would leave it with not even the fragment of its jurisdiction which it is proposed to preserve by this Bill. Now I do' not say that the Supreme Court of Canada is perfect; I do not say that the selections to the bench of that court have always been such as commended themselves in every way to all the people in tiie country. I admit that there is what you might call the inherent weakness that I have mentioned. But still, I say that the Supreme Court of Canada has in many respects done fairly good work; and if appointments of the most eminent men to be found in Canada are made to the bench of that court, It is capable in future of doing even better work than it has done in the past. I do not think that a measure of this kind ought, at least, to be passed by this House without more consideration not only from the House but from the government than that which this Bill apparently has received at the present time. It is a Bill of the most important character and I would suggest to my hon. friend the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) that if the Bill has not already been fully considered by the government perhaps it might be wise to allow it to stand in order that it may be considered and in order that we may have the views of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick.) in regard to it.

I perhaps might take exception to the statement of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) that the government will permit this Bill to be passed without any objection. Being a layman I will not presume to discuss the merits of the Bill, but the hon. Solicitor General (Hon. Mr. Carroll) in the absence of the hon. Minister of Justice, gave expression to his views of the government against the Bill and we were about to call for the division when the hon. member for Uabeile (Mr. Bou-75
rassa) rose and continued the debate. So that, there is no reason for saying that the government has not fully considered the matter. I am aware that the hon. Minister of Justice has advised that it is inexpedient that this Bill should be adopted at the present time. The government are prepared to take that view, and I hope the hon. member for St. Johns and Iberville (Mr. Demers) will not press the Bill at the present stage. But, if he is obliged to do so, all I can say that we will have to ask the House to reject the Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to discuss the merits of the Bill but there was one remark which fell from the lips of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) which I think should not go unchallenged. He has drawn a comparison between the Supreme Court of the United States and the courts in this Dominion and he made the statement that so far as his information was concerned the federal court in the United, States was one that was above criticism. I think that the hon. member has not been familiar with the history of that court. He has not been familiar with the decisions of the federal court of the United States. Many hon. members, especially those in the legal profession, recollect the Dred Scott case, the legal tender case and many other cases involving the question of slavery and a very notable case, that of the contention between Hayes and Tilden, candidates for the Presidency of the United States. On the contrary that court has been subject, and subjected, to very great citicism in the years in which it has been in existence. I do not think it is a matter of very great remark that ought to be emphasized but it only goes to show that it is impossible to constitute a tribunal that would be above criticism. The courts of this Dominion are not subjected to very great criticism, I think, in comparison with other courts and they are not entitled to greater criticism than are courts in other jurisdictions. I simply call the attention of my hon. friend to the circumstances with the view of repelling the idea that there is even one court in the United States which stands superior and above any court in this Dominion.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that diversity is one of the elements of beauty. I believe also, judging by this debate, that by an assimilation of races as well as by a uniformity of laws in this Dominion, our country would lose much of its attractiveness. Although the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) has stated that the government wanted this Bill to be rejected, I for one, will be obliged to vote against the government, much to my regret, because I entirely agree with the views so ably expressed by my hon. friend from St. Johns and Iberville (Mr. Demers). The members of this House are



not passing judgment on the Supreme Court. We might appeal to a much higher authority than to that of the members of this House. We can quote the judges of the Supreme Court against themselves. Let me take the dictum of Mr. Justice Girouard himself. I find by reference to ' Hansard ' of 1881, that he was the father of a Bill quite similar to the one introduced by the hon. member for St. Johns and Iberville ; in fact, I think the two Bills are exactly the same. It is true that, to-day, Mr. Justice Girouard, one of the legal luminaries of this Dominion, is sitting on the bench of the Supreme Court. But what was his opinion in 1881 ?
What will be my hon. friend's opinion when he occupies a seat on that bench 1
Wait till the clouds roll by. Let us stand by what we are discussing now.
Think of the future.

I see that Mr. Justice Girouard, speaking in 1881, after having quoted the section of the British North America Act as follows
The parliament of Canada may, notwithstanding anything in this Act, from time to time, provide for the constitution, maintenance, and organization of a general court for Canada, and for the establishment of any additional courts for the better administration of the laws of Canada.
makes this comment:
It seems to me that it is more than doubtful that this parliament had a right to establish a provincial Court of Appeal. The provision is to the effect that we shall have a right to establish a general Court of Appeal for Canada. We have made it general for the Dominion, and we have also made it a general Court of Appeal for the provinces. We have made it a Court of Appeal for the province of Quebec, contrary to the provision wjiich I read a few moments ago, which says that provincial courts shall be established by provincial legislatures. This is to me apparent, when we read the last words of the same clause providing for the establishment of any additional court, which would seem to be in the same spirit and sense, that is to say, for the better administration of the laws of Canada, not for the administration of the laws of the provinces; not for the administration or interpretation of property and civil right, or provincial rights. As I said in opening, I contend the Supreme Court is a necessity in constitutional cases, and that was also noticed at the time of the discussion of the Confederation Act before the imperial parliament.
Now, Mr. Justice Girouard is not tbe only one to hold such views. Sitting beside that learned judge on the Supreme Court bench we find the ex-Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Mills), a very high authority on constitutional questions. ' Hansard ' is indeed very useful in a discussion of this kind, as I find that in 1875 Mr. Mills said :

It seemed to him that this expression * a General Court of Appeal for Canada,' meant a court of appeal having cognizance of questions arising under the legislation of this parliament and not on any question that might arise under the jurisdiction of any one of the provinces.
You will also find, presiding over that court, a gentleman created Chief Justice, by this government, which I am sorry to say will ask this Bill to be rejected, Sir Elzear Taschereau, who, speaking in 1875, a long time ago, said :
In a word, they have their good old French laws which had been secured to us by solemn treaties, laws of which they were so proud, and under which their forefathers had lived so happy, and he might add, so loyal, under the protection of the British Crown. All these laws had a few years ago been codified by the most eminent jurists of their province, and at the present time their two codes of civil law and of civil procedure could well bear the comparison with the French modern Napoleon codes. The English speaking citizens of Lower Canada had long been accustomed to see their civil rights governed by these laws, they had learned to admire and cherish them, and they were now perhaps, as firmly attached to them as the French Canadian population was. In fact he hoped to see the day when all their sister provinces, seeing the perfectness of their codes, would adopt them as their laws of the land. But the more they were attached to their dear old laws, to their own legal machinery, so different, so widely different from the system of the other provinces, the more they were inclined to see a danger in all innovations proi not going too far when he said that when a supreme tribunal of appeal was proposed to be created outside their province, composed of judges, the great majority of whom would be unfamiliar with the civil laws of Quebec, which tribunal would be called upon to revise and would have the power to reverse the decisions of all their Quebec courts, there was, for them at least, cause for alarm if not a danger, a great danger to be apprehended.
We therefore have the opinion of three of the most distinguished judges of the land; nay, three judges of the Supreme Court
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon ; Mr. Justice Taschereau whose opinion he quotes is Mr. Justice Taschereau of Montreal ; not Mr. Justice Taschereau of the Supreme Court.
Yes, I believe the Solicitor General is right. He is a cousin of Sir Elzear any way.
Oh.
He belongs to the same distinguished family.
They are all judges in that family.

At all events we have a majority in our favour. We have two judges of the Supreme Court: Mr. Justice Girouard and Sir. Justice Mills both of whom not so long ago stated that in their opinion the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court was un-

constitutional as regards the interpretation of the Civil Laws. Having the authority of judges who themselves have contested their jurisdiction, and the Supreme Court being intended to be essentially a federal court-quite recently the court was asked for an interpretation of subsection 4 of section 51 of the British North America Act-should not the government support the Bill which has been introduced by the hon. member for St. Johns and Iberville (Mr. Demers) ?
Motion for second reading of Bill negatived on division.

MONK (Jacques Cartier) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 53) respecting Insolvency. He said : Mr. Speaker, in proposing the second reading of this important measure I have to express my regret once more that it has not fallen into abler hands than mine. But coming as I do from a city where we have very considerable commercial transactions it is perhaps not inappropriate that I should move in the matter. I know the trouble that was taken with this Bill when it was first introduced by my former colleague, now Mr. Justice Fortin, who with others took great pains in the preparation of the Bill, and who obtained the sanction of the commercial bodies throughout the Dominion and the approval of many legal gentlemen.

This is a Bill on which a great number of the members of the House who are not present tonight would like to speak. Would my hon. friend object to have it stand,-I ask him in the interest of those who are in favour of the Bill.

I would have no objection but for the fact that now we have little time left for the consideration of Public Bills. If I had the assurance of the government that this Bill would be discussed during the present session, there would be no difficulty in allowing it to stand. Private members now have only Mondays at their disposal, and the Order may not be reached again. I think the Bill should get its second reading now and we can consider it in committee later on. I would be very glad to see a larger House when such an important measure is being discussed, but, if I allow this opportunity to pass I have a fear that it will meet the fate that several Insolvency Bills have met with before 1896 and since.

To be candid with my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) I do not think he can expect to get his Bill through the present session. I could give him the assurance without hesitation, that there will be another Monday left when his Bill will be reached, if that is what my hon. friend 751	,
means. What would happen after that I cannot say. In view of the condition of the Order Paper, I would not lead my hon. friend to believe that there would be a possibility of the Bill going through all its stages this session, but an opportunity for discussing it will occur next Monday.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: That is not a very hopeful view which the Minister of Finance presents. This is a Bill which I think commends itself to the consideration of this House because it is the result of the study and experience of the men who are most interested in the administration of the insolvency law. It does not come to the consideration of the House at that stage in which measures often do, because hon. gentlemen will see that the Bill has been very carefully elaborated, and though I do not claim it is perfect in its present stage, yet it deserves to he experimented with.
Is it the same Bill that was introduced by Mr. Justice Fortin when he was a member of this House ?

Yes. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I think this Bill meets a want which has been very long felt in the country, and which it is imperative that parliament should supply. Almost immediately after the repeal of the Insolvency law, in 1875, boards of trade throughout the country urged upon the government of that day the necessity of some new insolvency law ; some law which would have general and uniform application throughout the country. In 1883 a Bill was submitted by Mr. Beaty, then a member of the House. In 1884 a Bill was presented to this House by the then member for Montreal Centre, now Mr. Justice Curran, neither of these Bills provided as complete an insolvency law as that which is now under consideration, because they failed to provide anything more than a method of distributing the assets of the insolvent. They made no provision for the discharge of the insolvent, nor for the penalties which are provided at the end of this Bill for the purpose of assuring an honest administration of the estate of the insolvent. In 1885 a Bill which had already been introduced once was reintroduced by Mr. Curran. Mr. Beaty also introduced a Bill which he had previously brought, to the notice of the House. In that year there was a committee of the House, which received the support of the Montreal board of trade, and I think of some other boards of trade. That committee prepared a Bill which was introduced in 1892, but which did not pass. Another Bill was subsequently prepared by the Toronto, Hamilton and Montreal boards of trade. That measure was urged upon the government of the day. In 1893 efforts were renewed in the same direction, and in 1894 the Bill which had been prepared was introduced in the Senate by the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, Sir Mackenzie

Bowell. That Bill received the consideration of a committee of the Senate, was discussed before that committee, passed the Senate Chamber, and subsequently reached this House, at the end of the session, but did not in. this House go beyond the first reading. In 1895 the same Bill was introduced in the Senate. It was announced in that year, if I mistake not, or in the previous year, in the speech from the Throne. The Bill died after passing its second reading in the Senate, and did not even reach this House. Another Bill was introduced in this House in February, 1896, by Mr. Martin, member for Winnipeg. That Bill did not pass. Every one will remember the circumstances of that session. The time of the session was occupied with one single measure which itself did not pass.
Coming now to the measure itself, which I have the honour to submit to the House, I will. not go into all the details, but will explain as briefly as possible the general scheme of the Bill. Let me say in the first place, that the courts which, under the terms of this Bill, take .cognizance of all insolvency matters in the first instance are : In the province of Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Manitoba and British Columbia, the county court; in the province of Quebec, the Superior Court; in the North-west Territories, the Supreme Court. As the House will see further on, there is an .appeal from the decisions of these courts to a higher tribunal.
Is that the same as in the old Act 1

things have been passed. The application is made after another notice given that it will be presented to the court for confirmation of the deed and the discharge. If, in the management of his estate the insolvent has in any way transgressed some of the penal provisions at the end of the Bill, or if he has dealt fraudulently with the estate, and it has been shown by the examination of the insolvent himself, or in any other way, it is an absolute bar to his obtaining a discharge. But, if, in every respect, his conduct has been that of an honourable merchant, and if he conforms with the rather hard conditions named in section 28, the court may grant confirmation of the discharge. The discharge granted under such circumstances, that production, of course, affects the reconveyance of the estate to the insolvent. Still, it is provided in one of the sections of the Bill, that, even after this reconveyance has taken place, if the insolvent fails to carry out the conditions imposed upon him by the deed of his discharge, the liquidator without any other formality-I may mention that there was evidently a great desire by the framers of the Bill to avoid useless cost and expense-may resume the estate, saving, of course, rights that may have been acquired in the meantime. Of course, when the discharge is granted and the conditions have been carried out, this operates as a complete relief to the insolvent from all the debts he owes at the time of his insolvency.
There is a provision against what has happened sometimes, the obtaining of a fraudulent discharge, or the fraudulent obtaining of deeds of discharge. Under section 40, it is provided, that wherever there has been fraud of any kind, or any kind of false pretense used in obtaining a deed of discharge, that discharge is null and void.
In part 3 of the Bill, provision is made for the liquidation of property. Costs incurred after the state of insolvency has been carried are not recoverable against the estate. Claims are proved by an affidavit. When supported by instruments in writing, those instruments have to be filed with affidavits in the receiver's office.
There are, of course, sections which provide for the application of the law of set-off. Privileged claims are set out in section 44 of the Bill. Remuneration of disbursements of the guardian, proper taxable costs of the liquidator, and arrears of salary or wages due, owing and unpaid to persons in the employ of the insolvent at the date of the insolvency for one month before, but not exceeding three months, of such arrears all claims for rent are provided for under section 59.
In the case of joint and separate assets, there is a provision in section 45. The debts of the partnership are paid in the first instance out of the assets of the partnership, and the assets of the partners are applied to the settlement of the individual debts of Mr. MONK.
the partners, and then to the debts of the partnership.
There are provisions with respect to secured credit where only claims of secured creditors are to be settled. These provisions are rather lengthy, and I will not read them, but I think they provide in an excellent manner for settling claims that are secured in such a way that the creditor gets the full benefit of his security, and, at the same time, the creditors of the estate who have not such security are provided against loss.
There are provisions also for dealing with conditional and contingent claims. I may say at once that these claims are valid as between the liquidators, and if these cannot agree after conference between themselves, the court is called upon to direct in what manner that claim shall be assessed or valued. The costs in a case such as this and other similar cases are to be left to the decision of the court. There is a provision as to the valuation of negotiable instruments upon which the insolvent is only secondarily liable, under section 46.
There are also some special provisions in regard to the laws of the province of Quebec relating to rights under marriage contracts in the province, providing that there must be registration of the contract a certain time before insolvency in order that the wife may be able to claim her rights. I think that is already our law in the province of Quebec. The liquidator has no right directly or indirectly to dispose of the estate in favour of himself, but his duty is to dispose of it under the direction of the inspectors, as soon as possible after he has obtained absolute control. He may provide, under one of the sections, in his own name for the recovery of all amounts due to the estate, and the costs in such a proceeding are to be charged to the estate. He may sell, with the sanction of the inspectors collectively, all the debts due to the estate, and persons who purchase these debts from the liquidator may sue for the recovery of these debts in their own name as effectively as the liquidator could have done before parting with these assets.
There are special provisions in section 59 in regard to leases, where the insolvent is a tenant of property. I shall not go into all the details of that section. It is sufficient to say that the privilege of the proprietor for the lien due him is preserved to him under the terms of the Act. A liquidator may give three months' notice to the proprietor that he intends putting an end to the lease, and the proprietor may claim damages in consequence of that, but the lease is brought to an end nevertheless. The liquidator also, in spite of conditions to the contrary inserted in the lease, and in spite of the provision that insolvency will ipso facto put an end to the lease, may dispose of the lease for the balance of the term. I think this is a wise provision, because very

often leases of that kind constitute a most valuable asset of the insolvent, and where there is a clause in the lease protecting the proprietor and providing that in case of insolvency the lease will come to an end ipso facto, the creditors of the estate of the insolvent are deprived of a very valuable asset which might be utilized by them without causing any prejudice whatever to the proprietor.
Special provisions are contained in sections sixty and sixty-one as to sales of real estate. In the province of Quebec we have, as you are aware, a special law in regard to forced sales of real estate. I will not trouble the House with detailed explanation of these sections, because I think they can better be considered in the Committee stage of this Bill. But I may say that so far as I have been able to discover, this provision in regard to sales of real estate in the province of Quebec appeared to me to be in conformity with the disposition of our own code of civil procedure.
As to the distribution of the property, there is nothing in this Bill which varies much from the provisions of the old insolvency law, and our own law as it exists at present in the province of Quebec. The dividend sheet is prepared, notice of the deposit of the dividend sheet is given by the liquidator, claims may be contested by handing in a contestation to the liquidator. That contestation may be admitted or may be opposed, and the documents constituting the record of the contestation are transferred by the liquidator to the court having jurisdiction in that case, just as it would in an ordinary case. There is an appeal from the decision of the court of first instance, just as is the case in our own province and in the other provinces.
There is a special provision in section seventy-seven. It is there provided that where a creditor is of opinion that he may take certain proceedings for the benefit of the estate, and the liquidator, creditors or inspectors of the estate are of the opinion that these proceedings are unwise and should not be taken, the creditor may apply to the court, and, on satisfying the court that he is acting bona fide, not in collusion with the liquidator, he may be authorized to take proceedings in the name of the liquidator, but at his own expense and risk, upon terms and conditions which are fixed by the court. In that case the proceedings are conducted by the creditor, and any amounts which he recovers under these proceedings are applied in the first place to the payment of the claims of the creditors who have taken such proceedings, and the balance, if any, is distributed among the other creditors. This is a new, and I think, a wise provision.
There is a part of the Bill devoted to the manner of the distribution of small estates. I think it is unnecessary for me to go into
that in detail at the present moment. There are several provisions in part five in regard to the duties of the liquidator, the security he must give, his inability to act until he has given that security, the time within which lie must give it, the register which he must keep of all his proceedings, his duty in depositing in a bank any moneys in reference to an estate he has under administration, his duties when he wishes to employ counsel, his remuneration; also for the proceedings to be had in case of the death or removal of the liquidator; also the discharge of the liquidator when he has completely fulfilled his duty and has rendered an account.
What is his remuneration ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS (Hon. VVm. Paterson).

speechtext:
This is what is provided in regard to remuneration :
The liquidator shall receive such remuneration as may be voted him by the creditors, or in default thereof fixed by the inspectors ; but if such remuneration is not voted by the creditors, or fixed by the inspectors, before the declaration of the final dividend or the preparation of the final account of the liquidator, If there is no dividend, if so voted or fixed, the liquidator is dissatisfied with the amount so voted or fixed he may apply to the court, giving notice to the inspectors of such application, and the court shall thereupon determine the amount of such remuneration, having regard to the nature and value of the estate, the work . done and services performed by the liquidator and the responsibility involved.
Are there any limitations as to the amount ?

No. In part six of the Bill there are penalties provided for persons who, being insolvent, being in the conditions which I have referred to when I began the explanation of this Bill, endeavour to defraud or obtain credit by false pretenses. Every such person is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment, or any greater punishment attached to the offence by any other statute. Are guilty of indictable offence also insolvents who do not make a full discovery of their property, as they are required to do the moment their insolvency is declared, who withhold their books or any of their property from the control of the liquidator, who conceal or secrete property, who do not disclose false claims made upon their estate, mutilate or falsify their books, make false entries therein, or dispose of property unpaid for. There are also indictable offences created in regard to creditors who obtain unduly and fradulently a preference against insolvents' property as regards, other creditors. A liquidator is also guilty of an indictable offence under certain circumstances provided in section ninety-one, which amounts to gross dereliction of duty.
In part seven entitled ' procedure generally,' there are rules provided as regards meetings of creditors. What must be done at the meeting. The chairman must be ap-

pointed, that chairman decides ail disputes, carefully prepared minutes must be kept, and it provides to what extent creditors may [DOT] vote. I do not think it is necessary for me to go into all details just now.

May I ask the hon. member (Mr. Monk) whether this Bill assumes any conflict of authority between the parliament of Canada and the legislatures of the different provinces and if it presumes to in any way repeal the Acts of the several provinces relating to the distribution of assets ?

In answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) I will say yes, to a certain extent, it repeals all the provisions of the local legislatures in regard to insolvency. As I understand it the provisions we have 1 in the province of Quebec are not strictly speaking insolvency legislation. , There are several enactments in regard to the distribution of the assets of a person who is not able to meet the claims made upon him when they come due.
Would not the same remark apply to the other provinces as well ?
Yes.
They do not claim to be insolvency laws.

No. We have, as I understand. absolute jurisdiction in matters of insolvency and that is why we begin the Bill by defining what constitutes insolvency, in what state a person must be to be considered an insolvent and therefore falling under our legislation. I suppose we have absolute jurisdiction to legislate as to what will be done when a state of insolvency exists, so tha,t I do not think there is exactly a conflict of authority.
It supersedes the provincial legislation.

We declare that a person finding himself in the condition described in the fourth section of this Bill is insolvent, we define insolvency and then we assume to legislate as to what would be done in the ease of a person who is in that condition.
If a sheriff under the provincial Act had charge of the assets of an estate how far would this Bill enable the liquidator to take that property out of the hands of the sheriff ?

I start from the principle that we have jurisdiction in matters of insolvency and the moment that state exists, even if the sheriff is in possession of the assets of an insolvent person, I assume we have the right to legislate and that the sheriff will conform to certain regulations mentioned in this statute in regard to insolvency.

The question is not as to the right of this parliament to Mr. MONK.	,
pass this legislation, but I think what my hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) is asking is if there is any machinery in the Bill of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) to deal with the case of the partial administration of an estate where there are provincial laws practically on the subject of insolvency although not professedly so.
Where there is a partial administration ?
Yes.
No, I think there is nothing in the Bill as to that.

There should be something in the Bill to meet cases of that kind. I refer to cases that we have happening in Ontario, probably in New Brunswick and certainly in Nova Scotia where we have been legislating on the subject of insolvency although we have not said so. I think this legislation has been sustained by the Ontario Court of Appeal. I do not know whether it has ever yet come before the Supreme Court of Canada, but in the province we have been practically assuming to do what this Bill is proposing to do, and the question is whether the Bill will deal with that condition of things to which I have referred, that is the partial administration of an estate, and whether it contains provisions for cases of that sort that may arise.
I think the Ontario Act in regard to the subject was sustained by the Privy Council. I would not like to be positive, but I think the original provincial Act was sustained.

I am not! quite sure. I have not followed the question for the last few years, but we have been legislating upon the question of insolvency and my hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) wanted to know whether the Bill made any provision in regard to the particular case I have mentioned.
I think our own legislation on that subject was sustained by the Privy Council, but I would not be sure. I do not think there was any provision in the Bill as it is now drawn to meet that case.

My question did not raise any doubt as to the power of this parliament to pass insolvency laws but it is only in regard to the machinery. I desired to know whether there was any machinery provided by the Bill which would enable an estate that has been partly administered under the laws of the several provinces to be taken hold of and the administration completed.
No. There is nothing in this Bill. It would be somewhat difficult to diaft such a provision.
It would be almost essential.

I think it would be very difficult, where proceedings had been taken

under provincial legislation for -Us to interfere. It may be done, but I cannot see bow it can be done very easily nor do I tbinlr it is very essential. We are legislating for future cases.
I do not think you could repeal their Acts relating to the distribution of estates.

There was a condition analogous to what the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) has mentioned ini connection with the Winding-up Act and the old Insolvent Act. Under the old Insolvent Act a bank could be put into insolvency. When the Winding-up Act was passed it was provided that where a bank was in process of winding uj) under the Insolvent Act the assignee or curator, or whatever he was, could apply to the court to have the winding up of the estate brought under the provisions of the Winding-up Act and the court might so order. From the time the court so ordered, the estate was wound up under the Winding-up Act and not under the Insolvent Act. It would not be very difficult to make some similar provision to meet such a case as that which has been mentioned.
Except that they were both federal Acts and my hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) is speaking of a provincial Act.

Quite so, but if this Act has the effect of superseding the provincial Acts then this House might properly enact that the winding up of an estate which has been partly conducted under the provincial Acts should be conducted under this Act.

There are provisions in respect to the jurisdiction of the courts, power of the courts to pass rules for the proper carrying out of the provisions of the Acts and appeals in certain limited cases. These are the principal provisions of this Bill, and I regret very much that, although 1 have summarized the Bill as much as possible, I should have taken up so much time. I think the Bill is entitled to a trial. It meets a very long felt want throughout the country. Our commercial relations between the different provinces are now very frequent, our commercial relations with other countries are increasing and I think' it would be of very great advantage to us to have one absolutely similar law on this important matter of insolvency throughout the whole Dominion of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose the government will have something to say in the discussion of this Bill and as I know that several hon. members who are not here would like to say something, and as the hour isi late, I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.

I am afraid that this Bill will meet the fate of previous insolvency
Bills. Is not the government of opinion that we might at least sanction the principle of the Bill, and advance it to the committee stage? We can discuss in the committee questions such as have been raised by my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) but I think we are able to form an opinion now as to the principle of the Bill.

I think there will probably be some discussion on the principle of the Bill. I do not wish to express any strong opinion on behalf of the government against the Bill, and the observations I made were not so much on the merits of the Bill as on the possibility of its getting through this session. My own judgment is that a Bill of this importance will never get through until it is taken up by the government. The experience of the past history of such legislation, which my hon. friend has referred to, goes to show that this Bill will only be got through when it becomes a government measure. The government has expressed no general opinion on the merits or demerits of the principle of insolvency legislation, but I am aware that the government is of opinion that such a measure as this can not be enacted during the present session. If the House desires to go on with the Bill to-night I have no desire to prevent it, but I am aware there will be some discussion on the principle of the Bill. '
Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
Do you want to sit any longer.
If we are going to sit any longer we might as well go on and discuss this Bill.
Unless hon. gentlemen interested in other Bills wish to press them I think we might now adjourn.

I have had a Bill on the Order Paper for the last five weeks, and I would Uke to have it get its second reading now so that it may be referred to the Committee on Railways and Canals. I have been sitting all night here with that intention.
I have no objection to sit longer if hon. gentlemen wish. We might take up non-contentious Bills.
I have no objection to that.
We can call the Bills in order and those not objected to can proceed. If any hon. gentleman is not ready his Bill can stand until another sitting.
I have no objection to that.

The question is whether a Bill that stands now will ever

do anything else than stand during this session.
Oh, there will be another chance.

Bill (No. 77), to promote the Safety of Railway Employees.-Mr. Smith (Vancouver) read the second time.
Mr. SMITH (Vancouver) moved that the Bill be referred to the Select Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.
I would like to ask the leader of the House if he intends to shut us off entirely. Surely we can say a few words about these Bills.
The understanding was that a Bill not objected to would go on, and that contentious Bills should not go on. I am quite willing to sit late if the hon. gentleman wants to.
So far as I am concerned I am glad that this Bill has passed.
It goes to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines.

As I understand it, there is not the slightest restriction on the discussion at all. By the unanimous consent of the House Bills that do not involve any discussion are to be taken. That can only be done by the unanimous consent of the House and there cannot possibly be any restriction of discussion on either side. Motion (Mr. Smith, Vancouver) agreed to.

On the Order being called for :
Second reading of Bill (No. 86) to amend the Fruit Marks Act, 1891.-Mr. Smith (Wentworth).
I am ready to go on with this Bill.
If the hon. gentleman does not object to let it stand until the next occasion, he will have an opportunity again without fail.
Very well. Order allowed to stand.

CHARLTON (North Norfolk) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 106) to amend the Act to Restrict the Importation and Employment of Aliens.
He said v At this late hour of the night and as the Bill is likely to provoke some discussion it might be advisable to allow it to stand, with the understanding on the part of the government that it shall be reached again.

I regret very much that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Mr. CHARLTON.
Charlton) requests that this Bill should stand. I have certain objections to this Bill and if next Monday is to be the only day on which it can be discussed, then I may not be here and I would like to have an opportunity of stating my objections.

I certainly have no objection to going on with the Bill, and under the point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) perhaps it would be as well to go on with it. Well, Mr. Speaker, the Bill which I submit to the House for second reading is a Bill for correcting a provision of the Alien Labour Law which bears with great severity and with great unfairness upon the manufacturing industries of this great Dominion.
Is it the intention to go on with this Bill at this late hour and with so few members in the House.

We have no means of preventing any hon. gentleman from taking up his Bill. We would prefer that anything that is debatable should be postponed, but we have no means of enforcing that if the House wishes to go on.

I am not anxious to go on with this Bill now, but the hon. member lor Elgin (Mr. Ingram) and the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Smith) I understand, raised objections to letting the Bill stand. My own preference would be to let the Bill stand, but if there are any members who want to discuss it to-night and who do not expect to be here when it comes up again, of course I am ready to. bow to their wishes and proceed with the Bill.

Surely, in the case of this Bill which is of vital importance to the interests of the working classes of Canada, the hon. gentleman will not proceed with it in the absence of the Minister of Labour (Hon. Sir William Mulock).
Those of us who may not be present again have the right to express our objections when we have an opportunity.

The Minister of Labour (Hon. Sir William Mulock) perhaps would be interested in this Bill; he ought to be here if he is. The laying aside of legislation because some member of the government is absent is a bad precedent to establish. I am in the hands of the government however.
Hear, hear.
You can go on with the discussion and adjourn the debate after those who wish to speak have done so.

In view of the wish of the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Ingram)
I think he should have an opportunity of stating his objection. The Alien Labour Law chapter eleven of sixty and sixty-one Victoria provides in section five :

Nor shall this Act he construed as to prevent any person, partnership or corporation, from engaging under contract or agreement skilled workmen in foreign countries to perform labour in Canada in or upon any new industry not at present established in Canada ; provided that skilled labour for that purpose cannot be otherwise obtained.
The amendment which I propose to this Bill will eliminate the words :
In or upon any new industry at present not established in Canada.
Then the section will read :
Nor shall this Act be so construed as to prevent any person, partnership, or corporation, from engaging under contract or agreement skilled workmen in foreign countries, to perform labour in Canada provided that skilled labour for that purpose cannot be otherwise obtained.
Now, Sir, this law which I propose to amend has been in operation for about five years. Manufacturers universally feel the burdensome character of this law. The provision that a man shall not be permitted to engage skilled labour that cannot be obtained in Canada is utterly absurd. It is an act of tyranny on the part of any organization whose influence secures that provision. The manufacturing interest of Canada is certainly worthy of consideration and of encouragement. There is a great party in this country which makes the cardinal principle of its platform the promotion of the manufacturing interest, which is prepared to give to that interest ample protection, higher protection than it enjoys at the present time. This Bill asks nothing of that kind; but it asks for a chance to have increased prosperity and increased development for the manufacturing interest of this country.
By lower wages.

Not by lower wages, but by the privilege of importing skilled labour-not ordinary labour or cheap labour, but skilled labour, and of a character that cannot be procured in this country. It does not propose to take from the skilled labourer here the employment that may be his due, but merely asks the privilege of importing that kind of skilled labour which cannot be procured here. This is a class of protection without increase of duty. It is a class of protection that will enable the manufacturer to increase the efficiency of his operations, to import improved methods and improved machinery, to bring here a class of expert workmen who can teach others in this country the methods in which they have been instructed in foreign countries. The great manufacturing nations of the world are all copying the improved methods which other manufacturing nations have developed, they are all bringing in skilled labour to increase the efficiency of their operations, to cheapen and increase production. Russia has developed an enormous manufacturing
interest in textile fabrics,_ in metals, in all lines of manufacture, and Russia imports English workmen, American workmen. American machinery. Russia has created a vast manufacturing interest by doing the very thing which this absurd law condemns and prohibits. The same is true with regard to Germany. Germany is importing American machinery for the manufacture of bicycles, for the manufacture of boots and shoes, for making pig iron, for rolling rails, for making structural steel, and is importing American skilled workmen to set up that machinery. The manufacturing industries of Germany have been revolutionized by the adoption of the very methods which this law will not allow us to adopt in the Dominion of Canada. I myself saw a German who was sent to examine the system of manufacturing pig iron in the United States, who said that the labour of ten men would produce more pig iron under the American system then the labour of twenty men would do in Germany; and his business was to look into the) system, to see what the methods were and the character of the machinery employed, and to make arrangements to import into Germany the kind of skilled labour which was not obtainable there. If this absurd law had been in force in Germany, such a thing could not have been done. There could have been no improvement in the methods of the German manufacturer, because the very steps to improvement would have been declared illegal.
What law was that copied from V

The English manufacturers have also been copying American methods; and where they have failed to do so, they have fallen behind in the race in many lines. Take, for instance, boots and shoes. A short time ago an English shoe dealer who had bought $50,000 worth of shoes in Chicago to send to England, was asked :	Why have you done that ?
Have you not as cheap labour in England ? ' Oh, yes,' he replied, ' Well, what is the matter ? '	' We have not the improved
machinery that the Americans have.' ' Why don't you get it ? '	' Because the trades'
unions of England will not allow that machinery to be put in operation. Not only will tiiey not allow us to import skilled labour, which we cannot get in Great Britain, but they will not allow us to use the improved machinery, and consequently we are losing our hold on the markets.' That is the work of the trades' unions in England, cutting off their noses to spite their faces, and doing more than that-depriving themselves of bread.
Not a thing in it.

Certainly there is. It is a palpable fact; and here is this law, maintained and upheld by the trades' unions

of Canada, which lays on our manufacturers the handicap of being unable to put themselves in line with their competitors in other countries, because it does not allow them to introduce the machinery necessary, or the labourers necessary to put that machinery in operation; but they are to be compelled to stay in the background, going on in the old rut, employing the old class of labourers and the old class of machinery, and playing second fiddle to other countries.
Is there any law in England which prevents the importation of expert labour ?

Yes, there is a law there, the law of brute force of the labour unions. We have not developed the brute force here, but we have the law on the statute-book, which acts just as effectively, and more so. As I have said, England's loss from the practical adoption of this policy is the loss in many instances of her progress in manufactures, the loss of her ascendancy, the loss of her ability to compete with her competitors, the loss in that keen race between the manufacturing nations which requires the nation which is going to forge ahead, to be permitted to use every instrument, every force, every improvement, every degree of skill, to range the whole world over to bring to herself all those elements of success which are essential to the consummation of her ambition. Special and skilled labour is a necessary thing in a country like Canada, where our manufacturing interests are not fully developed, our manufacturers can only hold their own against the manufacturing interests of the great nation to the south by being permitted to use the best methods to secure the best labour, by being entirely untrammelled in their operation and efforts to secure ascendancy or at least abiltv to compete.
Have they not an alien labour law in the United States ?
They have no such law as this, forbidding the importation of skilled labour.
It is the same law.

It does not matter. If a manufacturer who has the plant and finds that he cannot get the labour to run that plant successfully, is to be debarred from bringing that labour in which he cannot secure at home, his operations are handicapped, and you are placing a restriction on him that is not only injurious to himself but detrimental to the interests of the country and the very association which is forcing this absurd provision on the government of Canada. I repeat that the provisions of this law are unjust. It is a self-evident fact that where a manufacturer requires skilled labour and improved machinery, where he requires any improvement that will tend to Mr. CHARLTON.
increase the efficiency of his operations by diminishing the cost of production, a law that prevents him from going out and securing the best kind of machinery and the means necessary to put it into operation, is unjust to him, detrimental to the interests of the country, and an absurd act of tyranny on the part of whatever force or element forces that law into operation. I shall not detain the House further, but ask concurrence in the Bill I submit. It is as follows :
Section five of chapter eleven of the statute of 1897, intituled ' an Act to restrict the importation and employment of aliens ' is amended by striking out the words ' in or upon any new industry not at present established in Canada ' in the tenth and eleventh lines of that section.
The second section will then read :
Nor shall this Act be so construed as to prevent any person, partnership, or corporation for engaging under contract or agreement skilled workmen in foreign countries to perform labour in Canada, provided that skilled labour cannot be otherwise obtained.
The question may be raised as to what is skilled labour and whether it can be obtained or not and how that is to be determined. I was discussing this matter with the lion. Minister of Justice, and I agree with him that if this amendment were allowed a second reading, it should be referred to the Committee of the Whole and that I should move that that Committee of the Whole should rise and report progress for the purpose of giving the hon. minister and the government opportunity to make such safeguards as they might deem proper. If the House will permit the second reading, it will open merely one stage in the matter and then whatever safeguards with which my hon. friend desires to surround his amendment, may be incorporated in it.

I do not intend to take up very much of the time of the House at this late hour, but am rather surprised at the hon. gentleman moving of a Bill of this character, in view of the fact that he himself is one of the commission, I believe, which intends going to Washington in a very short time. I remember the hon. gentleman finding fault some years ago with the government for taking off the duty on corn, because In so doing they had taken a very strong argument out of the mouth of the Canadian ministers for getting something which would be of advantage to the people of Canada. He is to-night doing the same thing himself. The present Act was before this House many years and defeated many years until public opinion became so strong that it forced the government to pass it. We all agree that it is an act of tyranny, but so is the law of the United States, and it became necessary for the people of Canada to pass this Act in order to protect themselves against an exactly similar one passed by the United States We were obliged to give the

people of the United States the same dose of medicine they had given us. When Canadians, who desire to go to the other side under contract to do skilled labour, are debarred from doing so, is it great hardship to the people of the United States that we should apply to them a similar restriction ? The hon. gentleman said there is no reason why we should exclude from Canada a desirable, intelligent skilful class of Americans who wish to come here and engage in the development of manufacturing industries. Well, the law of Canada does not prevent any skilled workmen coming here. But what we do prevent is their coming in under contract, and we have a right to do this, at least until our hon. friend goes to Washington and persuades the Americans to remove the restrictions they now impose on Canadian workmen. I listened to tlie hon. gentleman's speech on the budget, and I find that in moving this Bill, he has forgotten what he then said. He then said :
If we propose to transfer manufacturing interests to this country as we are doing, and will do to a still greater extent if our tariff is changed in the direction of protection, it will he necessary in some cases to permit these American manufacturing interests to import skilled labour, and why we should impose this handicap in existing circumstances on our manufacturing interests I am at a loss to understand. It should be our aim and object to develop the resources of Canada, to increase its wealth in all lines of business in the country, and especially manufacturing interests.
Using the hon. gentleman's words, I am at loss to understand why, ' If we propose to transfer American manufacturing interests to this country, as we are doing and will do to a still greater extent if our tariff is changed in the direction of protection-*'
I want our manufacturers to be allowed to import skilled labour.
If the hon. gentleman's contention be correct, if we want more protection, and if that would be the means of bringing in manufacturing interests from the United States, I ask him to be consistent.
Will they not have to bring their skilled labour ? Will they bring Dagoes here ?

This is nothing about the increasing of protection. Raising the tariff is the only means for that. It does not mean that the fact of skilled workmen coming into this country is going to increase our manufacturing interests. So I say the hon. gentleman (Mr. Chariton) is inconsistent in this, as he is in other lines. I do not wish to take up more time, for it is late. But I say, in the words of the hon. gentleman, skilled workmen would be biting off their noses to spite their faces if they allowed a Bill like this to pass the House. For the reasons I have stated, the only protection they have is to hold this present law until
the obnoxious section is removed from the law of the United States. And I would say, in conclusion, that if the hon. gentleman from North Norfolk is to be one of the Canadian commissioners at Washington, I would urge him to use his best efforts to have the United States authorities remove that section. So far as I am concerned as a Canadian, I shall be glad to support a measure of this kind after such action has been taken by the United States. I do not believe in legislation of this kind, but we are simply compelled to keep it on our statute-book to protect ourselves against the injustice of the American people at this particular time. I do not wish to occupy time at this late hour, so I move the adjournment of the debate.

I think it would be better to refer the Bill to the Committee of the Whole House, with the understanding that a motion shall be made that the committee rise and report progress. Then we can consider the Bill in committee. That was the understanding of the Minister of Justice.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) to say that the Minister of Justice has approved of this Bill ?

No ; I do not say he was opposed to it. What I say is that he suggested the course that I now propose, that the Bill pass its second reading and be referred to the committee, and that then the motion be presented that the committee rise and report progress, and leave the Minister of Justice to consider the Bill, and the Bill to be dealt with in committee.

I think it would be better to carry out the understanding that at the conclusion of the speech of the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) the debate should be adjourned. There are several hon. gentlemen who wish to speak on the main question. Wre should not make progress at this late hour by continuing the discussion.
Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved the adjournment of the House.
What business may we expect to-morrow ?

On the list of Public Bills a Bill standing in my name follows that of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). There are also three other Bills. From the Orders of the Day it would appear that none of these four Bills have been printed, and so could

not be taken up. But X find, by referring to my file, that all these Bills are there printed. It would seem that a course of this kind would prevent Bills coming forward in due course, and, perhaps, delay altogether their passage through the House. I was wondering why this should occur- why the Bill should be on the file, yet that it should appear from the Orders of the Day that they are not printed.

I can ouly guess at the reason, and that is that these Bills were printed to-day after the Orders of the Day for this sitting were printed, and immediately placed on thes tiles. If that is not the explanation, I could not offer any. In answer to my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Borden), as to the business for to-morrow, there are several Bills on the Government Orders which will be taken up, and, after that, Supply; the Minister of Public Works again bringing forward his estimates.

Before the adjournment is carried, as I do not wish to take either the government or the House by surprise, I desire to give notice that the next time a motion is made for Committee of Supply I shall bring up for debate the matter of the position of the commander of the militia, especially with reference to some speeches and interviews recently given by Lord Dundona'ld.
Will the motion the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bourassa) intends to make occupy some time ?

It is not a motion, but simply the discussion of a matter which I wish the government and the House to take notice of. As the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cas-grain) knows, such a discussion need not be followed by a motion-

In that case, I beg leave to give notice to the government that the next time there is a motion to go into Committee of Supply I will move a resolution regarding the passing of certain Orders in Council relating to the Treadgold concessions in the Yukon.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.10 a.m., Tuesday.
